title: What we heard in powerful testimony from witnesses at NDIS inquiry
text:
Not since it was first set up, have the people who rely on and work within the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) faced such significant changes.

The government has proposed a suite of amendments to the laws that govern the scheme, which they say will reduce its cost by more than $30 billion over four years.

Over six days of hearings, senators scrutinised those changes asking how people with disability will be affected, what the impact will be on their families and carers, and what other services will be available to those who lose support.

Labor senator Ellie Whiteaker and Greens senator Jordan Steele-John listen to evidence on the final day of public hearings in the NDIS inquiry. (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

If the changes are made, modelling points to more than 300,000 participants exiting the scheme or being prevented from joining it, so there was not much common ground during the inquiry between what the government wants and the people at the heart of the scheme.

But there was agreement from witnesses across the board that rorting of the system must stop and the scheme's growth must be brought under control so that it can be sustained into the future.

The Senate committee only took submissions for two weeks, but in that time 4,500 groups and individuals wrote in with their concerns.

Among the submissions was a stinging rebuke from state and territory ministers who said the pace of change was too fast, they had not been suitably consulted, and alternative services would not be ready.

There were a number of contentious issues that came up over the hearings. Here's what we heard:

The cut labelled a 'safety issue'

The government has said NDIS funding for participants to engage with their community is a 'runaway' cost that needs to be reined in.

Their plan is to use a provision in the amended legislation that would allow the Commonwealth disability minister of the day to order a percentage cut to any stream of funding they see fit.

Once the legislation passes, the government has said the funding stream used by participants to hire support workers to get out into the community for things like doctors appointments, or to the supermarket, will be cut by 50 per cent.

Participants' budgets for capacity building (which fund therapies) will also be reduced by 10 per cent.

Federal Disability Discrimination Commissioner Rosemary Kayess is worried reduced funding for community participation could isolate participants and put them at risk. (Supplied: AHR)

Disability Discrimination Commissioner Rosemary Kayess said the cuts would mean many participants could find themselves stuck in unsafe environments like those exposed by the Disability Royal Commission.

"They end up in either closed environments or isolated environments, and they are at risk of violence, abuse and exploitation," she said.

A lived-experience witness said cutting his funding would have a profound impact on his life.

"If this government reduces that community and social participation funding any further, I effectively become a prisoner in my own home," Andrew told the hearing.

No one wants fraud in the scheme

One of the government's main motivations for the sweeping changes is stamping out rorts perpetrated by unscrupulous operators who exploit NDIS participants' packages.

Many witnesses told the inquiry they supported measures that would reduce fraud, overcharging, over-servicing and other sharp practices.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) told the hearings the scheme is an attractive target to criminals due to the scale of expenditure.

The most contentious parts of the NDIS bill With thousands of submissions made to the Senate inquiry into the NDIS bill, these were the most contentious of the changes proposed.

The proposed changes to the NDIS Act would give the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) the power it needs to investigate fraud on its own and address some conflicts of interest.

Several witnesses questioned why the bill did not go further.

"Given that the narrative has been fraud is a significant driver of cost, then this legislation doesn't necessarily go close enough to that," Bronwyn Morris Donovan, from Allied Health Professions, said.

Concern for carers

By providing support for people with disability, the NDIS has made it possible for many family members and carers to access assistance to manage their children's conditions or return to work.

The new legislation could change that.

The draft bill says parents should be responsible for providing "substantial care" such as the personal care, transport and behavioural support that "would reasonably be expected of a parent of a child of a similar age".

Skye Kakoschke-Moore, CEO of Children and Young People with Disability Australia, warns of potential for carer burnout. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The chief executive of Children and Young People with Disability Australia, Skye Kakoschke-Moore, said raising children with disability was not the same as raising children without disability.

"Expecting a parent to single-handedly provide the same level of care and support as a team of skilled, qualified, experienced support workers, risks putting that family into further crisis and may lead to increased instances of carer burnout," Ms Kakoschke-Moore said.

The government has said it wants to move children with autism and developmental delay, with mild to moderate support needs, off the NDIS.

The Thriving Kids program, which is due to begin rolling out in just eight weeks, will provide parents of these children with state-based support.

Advocates raised concern about how few of those services are in place yet.

Draft ministerial powers labelled 'dangerous'

Throughout the hearings there was condemnation from advocates for the proposal to give the NDIS minister the power to cut any NDIS funding stream they deem too costly.

George Taleporos has raised concerns about changes to ministerial powers. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Dr George Taleporos, a disability advocate who was instrumental in designing the NDIS, said the provision would create "a terrifying and dangerous power that will cause harm to disabled people".

Ms Kayess said the ministerial powers were very broad and lacked accountability and parliamentary oversight.

Naomi Anderson, from Villa Manta Disability Rights Legal Service, said putting so much power in one person's hands was a problem.

"We don't know who that person will be in future. We don't know what their budget priorities will be. We're basically giving them the PIN number to the bank account," she said.

What's next?

The inquiry will report back on Friday, August 14.

After that, the Senate will vote on the bill.

The Labor-led committee has already issued an interim report, which provides some idea of their thinking.

It said there should be clarification of how the minister is required to consider participants' safety when deciding to cut funding.

How did the NDIS get so expensive? With more changes surrounding the NDIS just announced, here's everything you need to know about the scheme.

It also called for more detail on "critical supports" that the bill says will not be impacted by cuts to particular funding streams.

It also recommended the bill be passed.

The government does not have enough seats in the Senate to pass the bill on its own, so it will need the support of the Coalition or the Greens.

The Greens and senator David Pocock said they did not support the bill passing.

The question everyone now has is what will it mean for the NDIS and the people who rely on it?

title: Doctors step up in bid to tackle Qld's 'hidden waiting lists'
text:
Queensland's peak medical body has taken matters into its own hands to try and address the ballooning "waiting list to get on the waiting list".

The state government consistently champions a reduction in the surgery waitlist, with just over 60,000 people waiting as of May, slightly down on the same time last year.

But the Australian Medical Association Queensland (AMAQ) noted the number of people waiting to get onto that list had skyrocketed to more than 362,000, up 15 per cent from a year ago.

AMAQ president associate professor Erica Gannon said a new task force will aim to tackle the issue.

Erica Gannon says AMAQ's aim was to work to find "sensible solutions". (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

"We know patients are spending months and sometimes years waiting just to find out what care they need," she said.

"This working group is AMA Queensland's contribution to finding sensible solutions that will support more patients being seen."

The six-member group, comprised of doctors across specialities and Queensland, will be chaired by former AMAQ president Dr Nick Yim.

"As a GP in regional Queensland, I'm acutely aware that local public hospitals are not keeping up with the number of patients being referred to them," he said.

The Queensland government’s performance on elective surgery Queensland's government declared victory on elective surgery wait times, but thousands of patients are waiting longer than recommended.

"We have incredible professionals working across our state, but as our population grows and ages, we are grappling with more complex conditions.

" Seeing hidden waiting lists continue to grow is alarming for patients who deserve timely and appropriate care no matter where they live. "

'Doing everything we can'

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie was asked why it was the responsibility of doctors, rather than the government, to address systemic health issues.

"The government's doing everything we can to reduce the waiting lists, and we have seen some success in that regard," he said.

"We've been in office for just over a year and a half. I think reasonable people, reasonable Queenslanders, would forgive us for being in office for a year and a half, tackling these big issues, where we are seeing the results coming through."

Jarrod Bleijie says the government is doing everything it can to reduce the waiting list. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Dr Yim highlighted the health system pressure felt in his hometown of Hervey Bay, symptomatic of strain across regional Queensland.

More than 14,000 patients were waiting to see a specialist in May, and almost 60 per cent of the most urgent patients weren't seen within clinically recommended times.

Dr Nick Yim says local public hospitals are not keeping up with the number of patients being referred to them. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi )

"That is almost 5,000 patients in Bundaberg and Hervey Bay in just a two-month period who weren't able to see a specialist close to where they live," he said.

"Sadly, across Queensland, it isn't much better, with 25,539 Cairns patients waiting for an initial appointment and over 45 per cent of Category 1 patients not being seen within the clinically recommended time.

"Central Queensland's wait list has jumped almost 46 per cent compared with last year while the number of initial appointments held has fallen 3.5 per cent, with only 38 per cent of all patients seen within clinically recommended times."

The AMAQ outpatients working group will deliver recommendations to the government in early 2027.

title: Hundreds of golden retrievers compete in regional SA
text:
Golden retrievers from around the country have descended on regional South Australia, going head to head in a competition of beauty and brains. Mostly beauty.

With nearly 300 furry competitors taking part in the 13th Golden Retriever National this week, there were just 60 dogs in the obedience categories, while nearly 280 tried their paw in the conformation rounds — the beauty round of the competition.

Janelle Salvestrin travelled 1,300 kilometres from Sydney to Tanunda for the event, bringing six golden retrievers with her.

Janelle and Brew came all the way from Sydney to pick up a couple of ribbons. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

One of them — four-year-old Brew — took out second place in the open dog class, adding to an already large collection of ribbons.

"He's a very successful show dog, he just loves it," Ms Salvestrin said.

As she got Brew ready for the arena, Ms Salvestrin and her team fluffed up his fur and gave him one last brush.

Brew loves holding his ribbons. Lucky he has so many! (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"I spend more on his products than mine," she said.

On the other side of the chilly Tanunda Show Hall, Sherry Jewell has travelled from Queensland with her team of four-legged champions, including one called Bruce.

At nearly 10 years old, Bruce is nearing retirement. But he still had it in him to take out the Winner of Winners category on the first night of nationals.

It basically means he is the best dog in the world. Besides all the other dogs in the world.

Sherry with Bruce, one of the best golden retrievers in the world. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"He's a very handsome dog and we love him," Ms Jewell said.

"He's done more than I could have ever imagined in the show ring."

It takes a lot of work to look as good as Bruce does, from nail trimming, to haircuts, to ear cleanses.

Dogs travelled from far and wide for the chance to get their paws on a trophy. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

But he does not mind one bit.

"He loves it. It's all about attention, and that's what a golden retriever is all about," she said.

"They're a beautiful breed, and they love to love you."

Secretary of the Golden Retriever Club of SA, which hosted the national, Ruth Thompson started getting her nine dogs ready six weeks ago.

Ruth and Roger Thompson, the proud new owners of a fancy ribbon. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"To actually prepare them for show day, it took me two days to do nine dogs," she said.

"They love the one-on-one attention. It's a bit like a massage to them."

Ms Thompson said it was pretty normal for entries in the conformation category to outweigh those in the obedience category.

The show dogs "love the attention" – and a camera. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"It's very time-consuming, training for the obedience at the trialling level, and it is hard," she said.

" They always do something for food and you're not allowed to take food in [the ring]. "

Everyone's a winner, baby

Judging between the greatest dogs in the world is no easy task, which is why they brought the big dog all the way from Finland: Marjo Jaakkola.

Ms Jaakkola has been in the dog judging business for 26 years.

"Especially if you find lovely dogs and nice quality, it's really a joy," she said.

Marjo Jaakkola, who has the hardest job in the world. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

And the dogs on show in Tanunda well and truly fit the bill, Ms Jaakkola said.

"I was really impressed with the quality. There were a lot of nice dogs and sometimes it was hair splitting making the choices in some of the classes because the quality was so good."

Ms Thompson, who has been breeding golden retrievers for about 30 years, said the judging assessed multiple factors.

This one was just awarded "best puppy dog eyes". (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

"It kind of comes down to the judge's preference as to how they think the dog fits the breed standard," she said.

"So they look at their head, their expression, their construction, the way they move, the way they carry themselves, their temperament."

title: Breaking: Royal show scraps bird and poultry exhibits amid rising H5 cases
text:
South Australia's premier agricultural show will be without bird and poultry exhibits after organisers decided to cancel those events amid rising cases of H5 bird flu.

The Royal Adelaide Show is scheduled to be held from Saturday, September 5 until Sunday, September 13.

The SA government said there had now been 119 confirmed cases in the state — up from 58 at the start of the week.

The Royal Agricultural and Horticultural Society of South Australia chief executive Will Rayner said the decision to cancel the bird competitions was out of caution.

"While we think the risk is very low, we took the decision now out of an abundance of caution to make sure that our volunteers and exhibitors had as much time to prepare as possible," he said.

Mr Rayner said the decision would impact about 150 exhibitors, volunteers and stewards in the poultry and bird section in particular.

"We know that numbers were already about 20 per cent down anyway, so people were sort of self-regulating and didn't want to bring their birds and animals in this environment," he said.

"The advice from the relevant authorities was wide-ranging about how we could best reduce the risk in the show.

" Ultimately, we felt at the show we couldn't comply with everything they were asking to do, and so we took this decision and we took it now so we gave people lots of opportunity to respond, rather than doing it in the throngs of the show. "

The Royal Adelaide Show will not have bird competitions this year. (ABC News: Bethanie Alderson)

South Australia's bird flu cases comprise more than three quarters of the national total of 155.

The government said the SA figure did not include deaths from a mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks near Robe.

Support for show's decision

The Department for Primary Industries Primary Indsutries and Regions (PIRSA) said it was working with organisers of other country shows to manage risk.

"We know that H5 is currently in wild seabirds," biosecurity executive director Georgie Cornish said.

"It isn't yet in poultry — we're very clear on that with people. We also know this is a moving feast."

Environment Minister Emily Bourke said the state government backed the Royal Adelaide Show's stance.

She said in the past 18 days the number of H5 cases in South Australia had increased from just five to almost 120.

"The Royal Adelaide Show took the difficult, but we think appropriate, decision to cancel our bird shows and exhibitions at this year's show," she said.

"Animal welfare and biosecurity is something that we take very seriously."

Mr Rayner said there were more than 26,000 competitive entries at the show and that birds were a "small part" of the overall program.

title: Meta ordered to pay $806m to address 'public nuisance' and child harm claims
text:
A New Mexico state court has ordered Meta to pay $US567 million ($806 million) to a teen mental health fund and change how its platforms function for young users after finding the company to blame for harming children's wellbeing.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid in Santa Fe ruled the company had created a public nuisance in New Mexico, siding with the state's Attorney-General Raúl Torrez, a Democrat.

Facebook paying white nationalist, anti-vaxxer Facebook is paying this Australian white nationalist to produce content.

Mr Torrez had accused the social media company of designing its products to addict young users and failing to protect children from sexual exploitation on its platforms.

Judge Biedscheid ordered the company to impose a range of youth-safety measures, including monthly limits on teens' use of Facebook and Instagram, restrictions on notifications, tighter controls on adult contact with minors, safeguards for AI chatbots, and enhanced review of child sexual abuse reports, under a decree that will remain in place for five years.

Meta said it will appeal the ruling and that it has been working to identify and remove harmful content from its platforms.

"We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts," Meta said in a statement.

New Mexico's Mr Torrez said in a statement that Meta chose profit over child safety and the ruling was the first to force a social media giant to make changes protecting children.

"This is not just a judgment against one company. It is a blueprint," Mr Torrez said.

"Now other states, and other countries confronting the same crisis, have a road map they can follow."

The ruling came in the second phase of New Mexico's lawsuit.

A jury in March had found Meta violated the state's consumer protection law by misrepresenting the safety of Facebook and Instagram for young users.

It ordered the company to pay $US375 million ($533 million) in damages.

Judge Biedscheid heard three weeks of testimony during the second trial over the lawsuit, which did not involve a jury.

It focused solely on whether Meta's platforms created a "public nuisance" under New Mexico law.

The case is being closely watched as states, municipalities and school districts across the US pursue similar claims seeking to force changes at the industry level.

Reuters/AP

title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
text:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

title: Dogs coach says he would have signed concussion waiver to keep playing
text:
As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

title: Council decides to sell off farm donated 'in good faith' to community
text:
A country council is facing intense scrutiny after deciding to wind up, lease the land and sell off assets from a beloved community farm once valued at $1.3 million.

The 596-hectare mixed farm known as Rylington Park was donated to the Shire of Boyup Brook by local farmer and community stalwart Eric Farleigh.

His only wish was that the property be retained "for the benefit of persons within the shire and for research purposes".

The property was run by volunteers for more than three decades and became a mainstay for community field days, shearing schools and agricultural research.

Rylington Park is about 30 kilometres south of the Boyup Brook townsite. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

The Shire of Boyup Brook took direct control of the farming enterprise in 2020, but earlier this year decided to wind down the operation by selling off assets and leasing out the property.

Retired farmer Richard Turner said the decision dishonoured the legacy and wishes of Mr Farleigh and the efforts of countless volunteers.

"He gave his farm in good faith … to see it going the way it is going is very disappointing," he said.

The shire said the "new management model" would ensure community cropping, research trials and scholarship funding continued in a manner consistent with Mr Farleigh's wishes.

Shire faces scrutiny

Mr Turner is a former chairman of the Rylington Park committee, which voluntarily managed the farm until 2020.

He said local farmers built Rylington Park into a profitable business that had combined assets worth about $1.3 million.

Richard Turner was involved with the Rylington Park committee for about 10 years. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

"Sheep were donated, the machinery was pretty run down … and over the years they got it up to running pretty well," he said.

By 2020, when the shire opted not to renew the group's lease, it had been running two community field days and eight shearing schools a year.

"We were putting through a hundred students a year — that's shearers and shed hands," Mr Turner said.

The council's decision to cease operations was attributed to the financial risk of a shire with a population of less than 2,000 running a large operation.

Most of the land will be leased, and all farm equipment and livestock will be sold by early 2027. The proceeds are to be reserved for a future attempt to restart the farm.

All livestock is to be sold by the end of January 2027, with all proceeds to be put in a quarantined account. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

But the explanation has received a mixed response from the community. The town's July 30 council meeting had to be paused due to repeated interjections from the public gallery over the issue.

Focus on farm's sustainable future

A spokesperson said the council was focused on securing the property for future generations while limiting the financial burden faced by ratepayers.

It said changing conditions across the agriculture sector had also had a significant impact.

Research agreements and trails at Rylington Park remain in place, but there are no plans to continue shearing schools. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

The spokesperson also acknowledged members of the community who were disappointed by the decision.

"The shire understands that community members have questions, and has sought to provide information through public council meetings, regular updates and community matter information sessions," they said.

"Our focus is on ensuring the community has access to accurate information and understands the reasons for council's decision."

Impact on legacy questioned

Mr Turner and eight other farmers the ABC has spoken with said the decision went against the charter of the farm and Mr Farleigh's wishes.

"They're not doing what Mr Farleigh wanted," Mr Turner said.

Eric Farleigh was posthumously inducted into the Royal Agricultural Society of WA's Hall of Fame for his pioneering research into improving soil quality. (Supplied: Royal Agricultural Society of WA/Felicia Lowe)

In response to public concern, the shire released a statement of support from Mr Farleigh's grandson David, a former resident of the area.

"I am satisfied the new management model as explained to me and adopted by the Boyup Brook Shire Council will retain the original intent of the gift given by Eric Farleigh," David Farleigh said.

"I am reassured Eric Farleigh's legacy and gifting of Rylington Park to the Boyup Brook Shire Council will continue his vision and benefit the local community into the foreseeable future."

title: Some of rugby league's truest believers await the NRL in Perth
text:
Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

A player's life at the outpost

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year. (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

The age of the Bear begins

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997. (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade. (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making. (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting. (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Loading Instagram content

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

title: Le Court wins Tour de France Femmes stage as Reusser keeps overall lead
text:
Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius overcame earlier difficulties to emerge victorious in a reduced sprint and win stage six of the Tour de France Femmes, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead with three stages remaining.

Le Court joined a small breakaway group 10 kilometres from the finish, launched her sprint with 300 metres to go and held off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands coming in third.

The 30-year-old Le Court suffered a mechanical before the final climb and had to change bikes, but, thanks to her teammates, made it back in time to launch her telling move.

"They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort," Le Court said.

"Then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front."

There was no change at the top of the standings after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, with Reusser holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney is third, 1:17 off the leader.

A group of three riders built an early lead of over two minutes but were brought back with 54km remaining.

World champion Magdeleine Vallieres set a blistering pace at the front on the penultimate climb of Col de Lalouvesc, which split the peloton, leaving a reduced bunch of about 30 riders to go for the stage win.

A group of six then got away, before they were joined by Le Court and Markus. The breakaway managed to hold off the chasing pack, and Markus made a move with one kilometre left.

The Dutch rider was unable to make her attack count, and it was left to Le Court to claim an almost carbon copy victory of her stage win last year when she outfought Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney in a seven-rider sprint to the line.

title: NRL and AFL 'saturated' with gambling and alcohol sponsors, report finds
text:
All NRL and AFL clubs have an alcohol sponsor this season, while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

The findings from the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (FARE) also show that both leagues have deals worth tens of millions of dollars each year with sports betting companies, which see them make money on every bet placed on their games.

The deals reportedly amount to $50 million per year for the NRL and $30 to $40 million per year for the AFL, FARE said.

SportsBet is a major sponsor of both codes as well, under deals worth about $10 million per year to the NRL and between $8 million and $10 million per year to the AFL.

With alcohol and gambling ads also becoming more prevalent in the leagues' women's competitions, FARE said its research showed these sponsorships were "deeply embedded across every level" of Australia's two largest sporting codes.

It comes as Labor's proposed crackdown on gambling advertising draws criticism from all sides of politics, with the Coalition, Greens, crossbenchers and some of its own party calling for stronger reforms during a Senate inquiry on the issue this week.

Labor's plan would limit gambling ads on TV to three per hour between 6pm and 8:30pm, on radio during school pick-up and drop-off, and ban logos on player jerseys or promotions in stadiums.

Labor MPs call for tougher gambling reforms The Albanese government faces internal pressure to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more MPs calling for sweeping amendments.

Alcohol ads cannot be shown on television until after 8:30pm when the media watchdog's designated children's viewing hours end, but an exemption exists for sporting matches.

However, the Australian Communications and Media Authority is currently reviewing that rule and is due to hand down a decision in the coming weeks.

FARE's State of Play report found that seven NRL clubs have gambling branding on their official playing uniforms this season — one more than the previous season — while betting advertising is part of 10 clubs' match-day promotions and across 12 clubs' digital channels.

Gambling sponsors are not on any AFL jerseys this season, but four clubs have digital gambling advertising and four clubs show betting ads at stadiums during matches.

Every AFL club advertises alcohol brands at stadiums during matches and through their digital channels, while five NRL clubs have alcohol logos on their jerseys and most clubs show alcohol ads in stadiums.

Every NRL club promotes alcohol brands through their digital channels.

Across the women's competitions, there are nine confirmed alcohol sponsorships for AFLW teams in this year's season and four for the NRLW, the report found.

Three AFLW clubs and seven NRLW clubs have gambling sponsors in the 2026 season.

FARE's research also found the volume of alcohol and betting ads during NRL and AFL broadcasts grew this year, with Seven and Nine both increasing their number of sponsors.

FARE chief executive Ayla Chorley said the report showed alcohol ads "saturate every part" of the sports and called on ACMA to take action.

Independent senator David Pocock, one of parliament's most vocal critics of Labor's planned reforms, has been calling for the government to implement all 31 recommendations of the Murphy Review — which includes a full ban on gambling advertising.

The Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs have an alcohol sponsor on their playing jerseys. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"We need a full gambling advertising ban — not some ineffective partial one that has been approved by the gambling industry, an end to harmful inducements and a national regulator to enforce the rules," he told the ABC.

Ex-NRL player alleges gambling staff offered drugs as he lost thousands Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs.

"Research shows that gambling and alcohol are huge accelerants to family and domestic violence.

"With 43 women murdered already this year, we should be doing everything possible to reduce and bring an end to this violence and the factors that exacerbate it."

Alcohol and Drug Foundation chief executive Erin Lalor said alcohol ads during sports broadcasting and at games influenced children and young people's attitudes towards drinking.

"Despite the significant harms that alcohol causes to individuals, families and communities, the alcohol industry continues to use sport to promote their unhealthy products," she said.

"That's why it's important to reduce children and young people's exposure to alcohol advertising, especially in the activities they love, like sport."

The NRL and AFL have been contacted for comment.

title: Country cafe mounting costly battle to retain beloved barista
text:
A cafe owner in southern Western Australia is facing an increasingly expensive battle to retain a valued worker amid uncertainty over the federal government's pending changes to the migration system.

Penny Hung has become part of the fabric in Balingup, about 231 kilometres south of Perth.

The town has a population of about 560 people and is thousands of kilometres from Ms Hung's home in Taiwan.

She has become a mainstay employee at one of the few cafes around, where she works as an all-rounder.

"I think for my personality, I prefer the country life," she said.

Penny Hung is working to secure a visa so she can stay in the small town of Balingup. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

"Balingup is very special; people here are very caring.

"It's very hard work to try to stay here."

Keeping qualified staff 'impossible'

Cafe owner Brian Foster said Ms Hung was a core part of the cafe, filling an important role in a town where it was hard to secure long-term hospitality employees.

"Keeping qualified people is impossible," he said.

" Penny's done so much training over the years, and she's an integral part of the business, and she wants to stay here. "

Mr Foster said he had begun the process of applying to sponsor Ms Hung, but the processing costs and minimum salary rate made it prohibitively expensive for a small business.

Brian Foster says Ms Hung is a crucial part of his business. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

It comes as the government moves to reduce net overseas migration, shifting its priorities for onshore visa applicants from skilled workers in regional communities to law enforcement and defence.

Balingup is about a 10-minute drive from the world's largest hard-rock lithium mine, Greenbushes, where Talison Lithium employs more than 1,500 people.

"Why would you work in a cafe in a village like this when you can earn that sort of money?" Mr Foster said.

" It's hard keeping staff when you're competing with something like that. "

Ms Hung is working to secure a solution so she can remain in Australia long term, having already used her working holiday visa.

Pay thresholds increasing

In 2023, the Australian government increased the threshold employers have to pay sponsored employees for the first time in about a decade, from $53,900 to $70,000.

Since then, the threshold has risen further to $79,423.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

Under the South West Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA), some concessions are offered to the threshold, as well as concessions for minimum standards of English or skills and experience.

That agreement is due to expire in December.

If Mr Foster were able to secure a concession under the DAMA, the minimum salary rate would be about $71,480.

Penny Hung is working to secure a visa to stay in Balingup. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

"When the original income was about $50,000, that was very doable for a small business," he said.

" It's a bit of a kick in the guts as far as immigration goes and sponsorship. "

Sponsorships 'expensive'

South West migration agent Maaike van der Zon said the increases to minimum salaries for sponsored employees in recent years had been significant.

"It's very difficult for some people to find sponsorship because it is too expensive or the salary level is just too high and especially for regional businesses," she said.

Maaike van der Zon said it was difficult for some people to find sponsorship when the minimum salary was too high. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson told the ABC that skilled visa income thresholds were indexed annually, in line with average weekly earnings.

"Indexation of income thresholds reduces risk of exploitation of skilled migrants, which could occur if there is a lack of wage growth and greater gaps between their wages and those of Australian workers," they said.

The full details of the government's looming overhaul of the migration system are not yet known, but the spokesperson said the latest ministerial direction would prioritise onshore applicants in order to retain migrants already contributing to communities.

"Under the new Ministerial Direction 119, employer sponsors in regional Australia in healthcare, education and now construction retain priority processing for applicants who are in Australia," they said.

Ms van der Zon said while a move to prioritise onshore applicants was welcome news for skilled migrants in Australia, she wanted to understand the impact on visa processing times.

"At the moment we're looking at seven, eight, nine months for those particular visas to be processed which are only temporary skilled visas," she said.

"We don't know yet where processing times are heading even with this new ministerial direction where they say they're prioritising onshore applications.

"We still have to see if that's really going to make an impact on visa applications that are currently in the system."

title: Queensland Audit Office criticises Townsville council rail yard project
text:
The Queensland Audit Office (QAO) has criticised the Townsville City Council (TCC) for its handling of a multi-million-dollar development in the city.

In a letter sent to Townsville Mayor Nick Dametto in July, the QAO said council had an obligation to report to its ratepayers on the financial operations of the council-owned company Northern Rail Yard Development Pty Ltd.

The company was created by the council in the 2023-24 financial year, which the QAO found was done without necessary approval from the Queensland treasurer.

The council said it was set up to oversee the redevelopment of a former Queensland Rail depot in the Townsville CBD.

The Queensland government has allocated $35 million to transform the North Rail Yards into a housing and commercial hub. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

TCC provided Northern Rail Yard Development Pty Ltd with a total of $624,000 in operational funding over the 2023-24 and 2024-25 financial years.

The Queensland government has allocated $35 million towards the project, which will see the railyards developed into a housing and commercial hub.

The QAO said its first audit of the council-owned company, which was dissolved in May 2026, found governance, oversight and financial reporting weaknesses.

"Resolution of these issues was not undertaken in a timely manner, resulting in significant delay of the completion of the audit," the QAO said.

"By the time these issues were resolved and the audit for the 2023-24 year was completed, council decided to wind up the operations of the entity, and it was deregistered.

"This meant we were unable to issue an audit opinion on the financial statements of the entity for that financial year."

In its letter, the QAO told the council to prepare financial statements for the 2024-25 and 2025-26 financial years even though the company no longer exists.

Townsville MP Adam Baillie (left), developer Brad Webb (centre) and Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki (right) at the North Rail Yards in March 2026. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"As the parent entity, council has an obligation to report to its ratepayers on the financial operations of Northern Rail Yard Development Pty Ltd including its financial performance and financial position for each year the entity operated," the office said.

The QAO also found that the TCC never received required approval from the Queensland treasurer to establish the company in the first place.

"This represents non-compliance with the prescribed legislative requirements applicable to council," the office said.

A council spokesperson said the absence of the treasurer's approval was the result of an inconsistency between the Local Government Act and the Statutory Bodies Financial Arrangements Act, and the requirement had since been clarified.

Company dissolved

The council revealed in a meeting in November 2025 that the LNP government asked TCC to dissolve Northern Rail Yard Development Pty Ltd in order to receive the $35 million in state funds.

Developer Brad Webb (centre) was selected to remediate contaminated rail sheds in Townsville. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The council confirmed Northern Rail Yard Development Pty Ltd had entered into a confidential development deed with Flinders St Rail, which is owned and operated by Townsville developer Brad Webb.

TCC said the company selected Flinders St Rail after calling for expressions of interest.

Mr Webb did not respond to requests from the ABC to comment on the compliance issues raised by the QAO.

Cr Dametto said the project was now being delivered under a direct partnership between the council and Flinders St Rail.

"The compliance issues identified have nothing to do with the North Railyards project underway today," Cr Dametto said.

"The project is being delivered by local developer Flinders St Rail under a direct agreement with council, not the entity referenced in the audit."

A council spokesperson said the governance aspects, raised by the QAO, related to the North Railyard Development Pty Ltd entity structure and its financial reporting rather than the project to decontaminate the site.

"Council now holds contracts with Queensland Treasury that provides funding to support the decontamination of the land."

Townsville City Council says it will provide additional disclosures. (ABC North Qld: Chloe Chomicki)

The mayor said the council aimed to ensure transparency with the community.

"Council will include additional disclosures in its 2025-26 Financial Statements outlining the funding provided to the entity," he said.

"Given that the entity no longer exists, officers are in discussion with the QAO on how this should occur."

Council financial statements for the 2025-26 financial year are expected to be released later this year.

title: Homelessness a visible crisis on Canberra's streets
text:
It is often dubbed an invisible crisis, but in one of Australia's most affluent and progressive cities, evidence of homelessness is becoming harder to ignore.

"People don't want to look at it, because it's gritty and it's hard and it's hard to fix," Havelock Housing chief executive Kylie Maiden said.

"But you only have to walk through Garema Place to see that it's not invisible — there are a lot of people sleeping rough in this city in very cold, cold winters."

Across Canberra, homelessness services are reporting an increase in demand tied to the cost of living.

Some people who use St Vincent de Paul Society's Night Patrol are sleeping rough in tents in public parks. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Vinnies Night Patrol hits the road 364 nights a year, with volunteers in vans supplying food, hot drinks, toiletries, warm clothes and bedding to those in need.

Last financial year, the service provided more than 19,000 instances of support in Canberra and Queanbeyan — a 38 per cent jump on the previous year.

The van's busiest stop is in Civic.

Angus Hutchinson says the Vinnies Night Patrol service often runs out of food items. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

"It can get up to maybe 50 or 60 people here, and we just end up giving out black coffee because we run out of milk," volunteer team leader Angus Hutchinson said.

The number of material items Night Patrol provides to keep people warm and comfortable overnight has also increased by 58 per cent in one year.

"People say that I'm only two pay cheques removed from coming out here," Mr Hutchinson said.

"I think everyone's feeling that lately."

Some of those who use the service are sleeping rough in tents in public parks, or in sleeping bags next to concrete buildings.

Others, like Victor, have a home in public housing, but are struggling to afford the essentials.

"I come out to get some food to supplement my diet. I do come here two or three times a week," he told the ABC.

Victor receives food from Vinnies Night Patrol several nights a week. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

The Early Morning Centre in Canberra's CBD is seeing similar demand for its breakfasts, lunches and emergency food packs.

"With the cost-of-living crisis, people are really struggling financially," centre director Nicole Wiggins said.

"[We're seeing] some new faces, but more of our regular faces … coming daily rather than weekly.

"We have people with university degrees, people who speak numerous languages, people who've owned their own businesses, owned their own houses, and then disaster has struck, and they've ended up on the street."

Data does not show a surge in the overall homeless population in Canberra, but ACT Shelter said the territory had the highest rates of persistent or chronic homelessness in Australia.

Corinne Dobson says worsening housing affordability is contributing to homelessness. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Chief executive Corinne Dobson said the housing affordability crisis was taking an extra toll.

"In terms of those who are accessing services … we've seen a significant increase in the number of older people, particularly older women," Ms Dobson said.

" We do see around 38 per cent of people who are seeking support are children and young people. "

About half of those seeking specialist homelessness services in Canberra have a mental health issue.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are vastly over-represented in the ACT's homeless population.

The Early Morning Centre in Canberra provides meals, practical support and human connection to homeless or socially isolated people every day. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Public housing shortage creating bottlenecks

Advocates say a big part of the problem is the ACT's long public housing waiting list, which currently has 3,600 approved applicants.

The average wait time for priority housing is more than five months.

For standard housing, people are on average waiting more than five years.

"You need to have a house to address homelessness," Ms Dobson said.

"As social housing continues to decline relative to population, those waiting lists are going to get longer and that really places a significant stress."

Ms Dobson said bottlenecks meant people were stuck in crisis or transitional accommodation for longer than they should be.

Havelock House, an affordable housing hub in Turner, is now receiving up to a dozen calls a week from people looking for a bed.

"I've been at Havelock for five years now and the increase is significant," chief executive Kylie Maiden said.

It can sleep up to 106 people, but Ms Maiden said the demand was forcing the organisation to reassess how it could use the facility to better support those in immediate need.

"The cohort that we see are the ones that are walking in from the street that don't have a home," she said.

Vinnies Night Patrol provides food and beverages, clothing, blankets, sleeping bags, and hygiene items to anyone in need. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Pledge to build more homes

The ACT government has committed to growing the Housing ACT property portfolio to more than 13,200 homes by 2030.

A government spokesperson said 364 properties were in various stages of design and construction as part of a range of territory and commonwealth schemes.

The recently funded Public Housing Pipeline program promises to deliver another 450 new public homes.

"This is a significant step forward that will deliver hundreds of new homes for vulnerable Canberrans now and into the future," the spokesperson said.

" But we know that demand for social housing continues to rise and there is more work to do over the coming years. "

While Ms Maiden welcomed the ACT government's commitment to build more public housing, she said it was only one piece of the puzzle.

"We need to look at service provision for these community members before they become homeless — so better access to mental health [support]," she said.

"You might shorten the [public housing] waitlist, but the waitlist will just keep growing."

title: Port guide: Visby, Sweden
text:
Advertisement

InspirationSweden Port guide: Visby, Sweden Brian Johnston August 7, 2026 — 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This article is part of Traveller’s ultimate guide to cruise ports. See all stories .

One of northern Europe’s best-preserved medieval towns is an absolute charmer, and sits over the horizon from the worst of the continent’s old-town tourist hordes. Who goes there Baltic cruises have become increasingly popular, and the cruise season has been steadily extended, with some ships now visiting even in winter. As a result, a wide variety of cruise lines visit Visby on Gotland, including Azamara, Celebrity, Cunard, Holland America, Lindblad Expeditions, Ponant, Princess and Scenic, among others. Cruises typically start and finish in Copenhagen or Stockholm, but sometimes further afield in Amsterdam or Southampton. Sail on in Almedalen Park in Visby. Swedish Tourism

Advertisement

The low-lying island of Gotland won’t provide much scenery from the Visby side, and nor will you see much of Visby’s fortifications and towers because (unusually) this medieval town doesn’t perch atop a hill. A huge silo on the headland will fool you into thinking it’s a castle for a while. In short, you won’t miss out on much if you’re intent on enjoying the breakfast buffet. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Berth rites Ships dock at a plain concrete quay two kilometres from the old town. A small shed-like terminal is the only excitement, and you may not be in it if your ship ties up on the open quay. The bigger terminal with the bridge arms is for disembarking passengers off ferries from the Swedish mainland. You could walk into town in 30 minutes, but free shuttles are the better option. There isn’t much point in the hop-on hop-off bus, since it can’t enter the old town. Going ashore The former Hanseatic league trading port and World Heritage walled city, overlooked by 27 towers, is where you want to wander. Some of the fortifications and churches are in ruins, but medieval Visby is otherwise very well preserved. It’s more about the overall picture and atmosphere rather than any particular buildings, but the Cathedral of St. Mary and the ruined Dominican Monastery are worth a look. The very good Gotland Museum covers 5000 years of the island’s history, and exhibits prehistoric carved stones, Viking silver coins, medieval art and more.

Advertisement

Don’t miss UNESCO World Heritage Site the Visby City Wall, or Ringmuren. Swedish Tourism Amid all the medieval architecture and cobbled quaintness, it’s easy to miss the free DBW’s Botanical Garden, which were first laid out in the 19th century. Although small, the gardens are delightful and showcase roses and exotic trees. A gate leads through the city wall nearby and onto the waterfront. Get active You could walk around the base of the medieval walls, which run for 3.5 kilometres, or stick to the promenades that meander along the waterfront. If you want to get further along the coast and around parts of the island, rent a bicycle. Hogklint Nature Reserve just outside town is a good place for walking, with views from limestone cliffs. You can rock climb and abseil, mountain bike and horse ride elsewhere on Gotland.

Advertisement

Related Article Europe Europe’s most enjoyable old town has no crowds and no fees Best bites Seafood is naturally foremost on an island, and on Gotland particularly smoked salmon, herring (often accompanied by potatoes and a cream-based sauce) and pickled fish. However, Gotland lamb is dished up in hearty stews. In summer, cloudberries, dewberries and lingonberries are a must-try. The dish most associated with Visby is a saffron rice pancake served with cloudberry jam, and there’s no lack of cafés in which to enjoy it. Further afield Although Visby is the highlight, Gotland island has plenty more for the inquisitive visitor, including unusual boat-shaped Bronze Age graves, Viking history, pretty churches and villages such as fishing village Gnisvard, and surprisingly wild landscapes. A typical excursion will take you on an island overview. Some cruise lines offer a local farm experience with tastings of local produce or insight into wool textile making.
