title: These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age August 7, 2026 — 12:54pm

August 7, 2026 — 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL commission chairman Craig Drummond was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision, when the Cats struck what has been acknowledged was an inappropriate waiver with a player who had a history of concussions. On Thursday, as the story detonated that the Cats had signed the player to a waiver that diminished his legal rights – at least on paper – Drummond was asked to respond to questions from this masthead, and doubtless other media, about his role in the shonky waiver. Craig Drummond’s brief statement does not address the questions that need to be answered about the concussion waiver Geelong signed with a senior player when he was the club’s president. AFL Photos via Getty Images The AFL chairman, who holds the highest office in the game, issued a brief statement that did not address the obvious questions that he should have taken on, given his twin hats as AFL chairman and the president of the club at the time that this hubristic document was signed, without the AFL’s consent or knowledge. Drummond’s AFL chose not to sanction Geelong, a matter of months after Carlton was fined $75,000 for their handling of the Elijah Hollands affair, which was about a different kind of player safety – mental health.

Advertisement

The AFL took weeks to sort through the messy Hollands imbroglio before settling on a sanction. They needed only half a day to rule that the Cats were off the hook. Drummond’s time as AFL chairman has won praise within clubs for the energetic reshaping of the commission and introducing the kind of governance – term limits for the board, most of all – that were not evident during the Richard Goyder era, in which Gillon McLachlan was allowed to run his race. Loading But, as with political leaders, AFL honeymoons are as fleeting as Essendon winning streaks and Drummond did not last the whole 2026 season without finding himself in political cow manure. His statement contained the clichéd motherhood lines about the clubs and AFL continuing “to prioritise the health and safety of all our players”.

Advertisement

Those words read as utterly hollow, since Geelong had not made the player’s “health and safety” their priority in the now-recanted part of the agreement. The whole objective of the waiver was to absolve the club of responsibility for the player’s long-term health (in relation to head injuries) and put the onus on the player. The only excuse for the Cats is that it would have been easier to not offer him a contract (the AFL concussion panel had cleared him to play). While it was the player’s initiative that this deal be struck, the Cats went off the reservation by getting him to sign away legal protections. Before he became AFL chairman, Craig Drummond was Cats president, He’s pictured here in 2022 with star Patrick Dangerfield after the club won the 2022 grand final. Getty Carefully crafted statements, without answering questions, is a strategy that could succeed for Drummond and the AFL given society’s attention spans, which are shorter than the time it took the league to clear the Cats. Drummond, however, has a responsibility to address questions about an embarrassing, ill-considered and furtive arrangement that has not – to my knowledge – been tried on by other AFL clubs. If an oft-concussed player signed a waiver or its equivalent in the VFL, before he was drafted on to an AFL list, that still falls short of Geelong’s too-clever ploy.

Advertisement

Drummond was at the helm of Geelong when this happened, and holds even greater responsibility now as AFL chairman. These questions, which he hasn’t yet padded up for, should be answered candidly, in full: Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player As president of Geelong in 2024, does he take responsibility for the waiver the club signed with the player? Do he and Geelong owe the player an apology? Why was this waiver necessary? Did any parts trouble him then? You’ve called Geelong’s changes “appropriate.” Can you clarify if you regret that you were a party to this arrangement? You say health and safety of players is paramount. Why was Geelong not sanctioned, for an arrangement that went outside the AFL and the AFL Players Association, and which will be disallowed in future? Carlton was sanctioned with a $75,000 fine for allowing a medically unfit player on the field. Please explain the vast gap in consequence for Carlton’s offence and Geelong’s missteps? Given the conflict of interest between your roles as Geelong president then, and AFL chairman now, how did you ensure that the decisions and discussions within the AFL were not influenced by your interests? What steps, if any, did you take? This episode underscores that Geelong’s greatness as a footy club has little basis in some imagined moral superiority of “values” and decency; the narrative some ex-Geelong players and officials unwisely spruik. Yes, the Cats are exceptional – in coaching, recruiting and development, not in niceness, humility and tender care. They come across as a ruthless organisation that makes hard calls and is focused on winning games, not friends or wellbeing awards. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: Hanson feuds with media, concedes using party funds for luxury hotel
text:

PoliticsFederalOne Nation Hanson feuds with media, concedes using party funds for luxury hotel Brittany Busch August 7, 2026 — 12:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has lashed out at Channel Seven, claiming the broadcaster pulled out of funding her travel expenses in the UK, and denied reports in this masthead that she left luxury hotel rooms in London empty while she travelled to Italy. Hanson conceded on Friday a key claim, first reported in this masthead, that she used party funds to pay for a stay in a $900-a-night five-star hotel in London. The One Nation leader, who is ascendant in the polls, travelled to Europe on a 10-day “fact-finding” mission in July, during which she filmed a program with Seven’s Spotlight program. Hanson spoke at CPAC GB in London in July. Luca Marino During the trip Hanson sat down with far-right agitator and criminal Tommy Robinson, and appeared at CPAC GB, a conservative conference headlined by Nigel Farage. Hanson admitted in a Facebook post on Friday morning that she used the party’s money, rather than her own funds, to pay for the luxury accommodation, but denied she had left rooms empty in London during a trip to Italy to meet mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.

Advertisement

The One Nation leader claimed that Seven pulled out of paying for the UK trip, obliging her to use party funds. Related Article Exclusive

Political expenses Empty five-star room: Hanson paid for $900-a-night hotel with party funds “Spotlight have been shady from day one. Original travel plans for the Spotlight episode were to be paid by Channel Seven. They pulled out forcing One Nation to cover all travel costs,” Hanson wrote. A spokesperson for Channel Seven said the broadcaster did not pay for any travel expenses for One Nation. “Seven paid for incidentals, including a vehicle used in the production process and a hotel room used for filming purposes as well as security to protect Seven staff while recording on UK streets, but no travel expenses for One Nation.”

Advertisement

Hanson’s attacks on Seven and this masthead cap off a week in which she on Monday barred The Age, the ABC and The Guardian from a Melbourne press conference where the party announced eight candidates for the November state election. Stating that “mainstream media publish lies”, Hanson wrote that she provided Expedia invoices to news.com.au journalist Samantha Maiden to prove she cancelled her London accommodation while in Italy. News.com.au reported Hanson had used interest generated from a $20 million donation pot to pay for the accommodation. A screenshot of a partial invoice published by the outlet appears to show five days’ accommodation at the Conrad Saint James Hilton from July 15. A screenshot, published by news.com.au, the One Nation provided the outlet to show the room rate and dates for a hotel room. screengrab/news.com.au

Advertisement

Hanson’s declaration of interests shows Rinehart paid for flights from London to Sicily via Rome on July 11 and return on July 16. One Nation told news.com.au the hotel was booked for an extra day because it did not allow an early check-in, and it was needed for a late flight arrival. The screenshot does not include the hotel name, Expedia branding, or the date the booking was made. It is also only for one room, not for the other staff who stayed at the time. “I can confirm that while I was in Italy, accommodation in London was cancelled,” Hanson said on Facebook. A source familiar with the trip told this masthead earlier this week Hanson left rooms vacant at the luxury London for days while she was in Italy with Rinehart, where she attended a Dolce and Gabbana fashion show.

Advertisement

Another source suggested the lavish trip had caused unease within One Nation because it was sitting on a fresh $5 million war chest from the viral Fire the Liar fundraising campaign, which had bolstered the party’s coffers off the back of ordinary Australians chipping in small amounts to campaign against Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. This masthead sent questions to One Nation over several days about the London accommodation. One Nation did not answer the questions or provide invoices, and only stated that the Fire the Liar campaign money was kept separate in a trust. Senator Sean Bell on Friday said he did not know how Hanson funded the trip, before saying it was not with the campaign donations. “You’re asking me to speculate on something that I have no knowledge about,” Bell told News24 on Friday. “That money that we’ve raised, for instance, with the Fire the Liar campaign, I know for a fact that that is cordoned off where it can only be used to campaign against this terrible Albanese Labor government. All the money that was sent to that is being used on that issue,” he said.

Advertisement

“I can assure people, and Senator Hanson assures people, when we go overseas, we do so making sure people get bang for their buck. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson had earlier accused Hanson of betraying her supporters. “We have people who donate to her party from their limited savings, they’re struggling to get ahead, and now we find it’s going towards luxury hotel rooms in London, Dolce and Gabbana fashion shows,” Wilson told Nine’s Today. title: Bunnings has sucked me in … and taught me some lessons
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyConsumer spending Opinion Bunnings has sucked me in … and taught me some lessons Millie Muroi Economics Writer August 7, 2026 — 11:59am

August 7, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m a sucker for all things cute and fluffy – not adjectives you’d typically use when talking about a hardware store. It’s probably one of the reasons I rarely swing by Bunnings. Type “fluffy” into the search bar on Bunnings’ website, and you get washing liquid, dog beds and rugs. All very practical, but not very appealing for someone who finds enjoyment in impractical things. I’m hoping these bears will be an unconventional type of investment. One thing (arguably of many) that I never grew out of is my love of soft toys. I have far too many occupying far too much real estate on my bed for someone who has been an adult for nearly a decade. Now, they’ve been joined by Bunnings-branded … bears. Basically, Bunnings has cracked a code that has allowed it to expand into some new markets. Think: children, collectors … and at least one twenty-something woman who doesn’t especially need anything from Bunnings – least of all, another soft toy with diminishing marginal benefit.

Advertisement

“Blind boxes” – sealed packages containing random collectible items – have been around for a while, but in recent years, they’ve really taken off. Labubus, Sonny Angels and Smiskis are some of the most popular ones globally. Local stores such as Woolworths (with its Disney-themed “Ooshies”) have understood this lure of the unknown for a long time, taking advantage of the psychology driving our decision-making in their sales promotions. For a while, I thought I’d escaped the hold of blind boxes: none of them really appealed to me. While blind boxes aren’t technically counted as gambling because you don’t, strictly speaking, lose money (you always get something in return), the psychology works almost identically. And, arguably, despite ending up with 11 plush bears from Bunnings’ line-up – including some duplicates – I like to think I largely evaded their blind box “trap” and snagged a bargain. Either way, there are several economics lessons I took away from the experience. It all started with exposure. Unboxing videos have become increasingly popular on social media, with influencers opening products they’ve ordered or been sent, including the growing range of blind boxes.

Advertisement

The first few times I saw the Bunnings bears, I didn’t think much of them. Cute, but not necessary, I remember thinking. But there’s something called the “exposure effect”: a psychological tendency for people to develop a greater liking for things – whether it’s products or even people – the more they see them. It’s one of the reasons companies pay for advertising. They don’t just do it to make customers aware that their products exist, but also to develop brand recognition and familiarity which makes us more likely to reach for those items when shopping. Related Article Good Weekend ‘You can tell the fakes by the number of teeth’: My counterfeit Labubu conundrum It’s one of the ways that what we might think are rational decisions are not always as clear-cut as traditional economic models might assume. Often, our behaviours are influenced in ways that may not be rational or optimal for our wellbeing. That’s why there’s a relatively new branch of the discipline called “behavioural economics”: the study of how psychology, emotions and cognitive biases shape financial and economic decisions. The line-up of different Bunnings bears – each with a nearly one-in-four chance of being “pulled” from any given box – was cute, but it was the one marketed as the “secret bear” (with a one-in-16 chance of being found) that caught my eye.

Advertisement

The “sausage sizzle bear” is a teddy bear wrapped in a slice of (fake) bread to resemble the iconic Bunnings sausage sizzle snags. Clearly, not everyone would be swayed by this as much as I was. But it’s a good example of the effect of nostalgia: another thing that can increase our willingness to pay. Why? Because nostalgia is often linked to happy experiences and a sense of security. Pairing the cute teddy bear – which many of us already link to nostalgia – with an experience many of us are familiar with helps increase its appeal … at least for people like me. Related Article Retail The new status symbol for Gen Z is not what you’d expect Bunnings also created an artificial scarcity by making only a relatively small number of some of the bears. Generally, things that are finder to hard, or limited in quantity, are seen as more valuable. That’s why diamonds or vintage items, for example, tend to sell for eye-wateringly high prices. This scarcity is also the reason that the “sausage sizzle” bear has much higher asking prices from sellers on second-hand platforms such as Facebook Marketplace, Depop and eBay.

Advertisement

Seeing the bears pop up on these platforms, I decided that rather than going to Bunnings and buying potentially dozens of blind boxes (retailing for $12.50 each) to find the one I wanted, I was probably better off buying one someone had already found – even if it meant paying significantly more. I settled for a sausage sizzle bear off Facebook Marketplace which was selling for $50: probably a better-value option than testing my luck with blind boxes and ending up spending lots of money with double-ups of bears I didn’t have a huge desire for, I thought. Of course, the appeal of blind boxes is largely the element of surprise: not knowing what you might get. While blind boxes aren’t technically counted as gambling because you don’t, strictly speaking, lose money (you always get something in return), the psychology works almost identically. Humans tend to enjoy a bit of uncertainty because it can boost excitement and trigger a bigger dopamine rush. Plenty of people have probably gone to Bunnings to buy these blind boxes for that very experience. From Bunnings’ perspective, they bring a lot of value. Not only does it probably make a tidy profit from them (the bears would cost much less than $12.50 to manufacture), but they also bring foot traffic to its stores from people who might be tempted to pick up a few other things while they’re there.

Advertisement

Collectible items can also drive consumption in other ways. When I first bought the sausage sizzle bear, I thought that would be the end. It was all I wanted. But the thing about collectibles is that they exploit psychological triggers such as completion bias: the tendency for people to feel compelled to complete something once they’ve started it. Loading When I found someone selling the full set of Bunnings bears for $60 on Facebook Marketplace, I jumped at the opportunity. Partly, it was driven by the idea that maybe, just maybe, it could be an investment. Most full sets I had seen in the secondhand market were fetching at least $100, and surely when the next instalment of bears is released, there will be people willing to pay a higher price for a complete set, I remember thinking. But there’s also something called the endowment effect: a tendency to overvalue (and justify) items once we own them. While I’m yet to see many people selling a full set of the bears for less than $100, it’s also very possible they will be worthless in a year or two.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Pay What Macca’s reveals about our living standards – and how to get a free lunch Millie Muroi Economics Writer Nonetheless, I also ended up buying a bear from the first collection of Bunnings bears (released last year), which then led to me buying another four for $30 from a woman on Depop. Part of me thought it could add to my “investment”, but there was also a part of me itching to complete the two sets. Awareness of these cognitive and behavioural biases can help us be a bit more rational in our spending, and bring us closer to the neat models of traditional economics, which are built on the assumption we always make optimal decisions. While there are a handful of the ultra-rare “hoodie” bears from the first Bunnings collection (which would complete my two sets) on online secondhand marketplaces, most of them seem to have an asking price of at least $150 as a standalone item. That’s probably not an optimal use of money for anyone, let alone someone with a mortgage. And even for an irrational consumer like me, I’ve decided that’s a bit steep … or is it? title: ‘Snatched’ in Turkey: How a gory social media trend is fuelling a surge in cosmetic tourism
text:
While Australians increasingly film their post-op journeys for millions of views, doctors are scrambling to build a national database to measure the strain botched overseas surgeries are placing on our healthcare system.

Joanne McGinnis always hated the excess skin on her neck. At the hairdresser, she felt self-conscious when the salon cape was fastened snugly, gathering the loose skin underneath her chin. “I hated looking in the mirror,” she said. “My biggest insecurity was my neck.” Joanne McGinniss paid $18,000 for extensive cosmetic surgery in Turkey. She is far from alone. In February this year, for her 45th birthday, McGinniss boarded a plane to Turkey. The purpose of the trip? “Getting snatched,” she said. She is far from alone. In the past 18 months, Australian plastic surgeons have observed a striking uptick in people travelling to Turkey for cheap, fast-tracked cosmetic procedures, including facelifts and hair transplants.

Advertisement

The surge in cosmetic tourism has spurred a troubling wave of post-surgical complications and an online trend where patients document their recovery process on Instagram and TikTok. Related Article Cosmetic Cowboys Crackdown on deceptive social media posts by cosmetic doctors In the “recovery diary” videos, patients who have travelled to the cosmetic surgery hotspot of Istanbul document their swollen, bruised, bloodied, bandaged faces, gruesome complications and emotional ups and downs in daily instalments. McGinniss said she shared her story online to provide insights on her recovery and tips on how to find a credible and safe surgeon. She said she is not paid for her content, framing it as a free public service to support anyone considering or recovering from cosmetic surgery. Her inbox is flooded with messages. “I can’t keep up, it’s like a second job,” she said.

The Adelaide woman went from 600 followers to more than 18,500 almost overnight. Some of her videos now have more than three million views. “The first few weeks were really quite difficult,” she said of her recovery. “I was like ‘holy shit! What have I done?’ Because you just don’t look like you and then every time you’re looking in the mirror, you’re questioning yourself.” Joanne McGinniss in the days after her extensive cosmetic surgery. But Australian doctors say they are increasingly having to pick up the pieces when these overseas surgeries go wrong. Australian Society for Plastic Surgeons president Dr Brigid Corrigan said in severe cases, doctors have treated permanently damaged nerves, dead skin, bleeding, wound infections, abnormal scarring and asymmetry that required revision surgery. “We are really seeing the full spectrum of complications,” Corrigan said. Concerned by this trend, the peak body has started to compile data on botched procedures and complications in a national database, which is also tracking hospital admissions.

They warn patients are being lured by cosmetic surgery packages that include five-star hotels and VIP airport transfers that allow them to squeeze in as many surgeries as possible within a short timeframe. Related Article Ageing A facelift under 40: Is it worth it? McGinniss estimates she saved about $80,000 getting her surgery abroad, spending more than a year carefully researching surgeons in Turkey before finally booking one in. While McGinniss said many people supported the online documentation of her recovery, she was trolled by a small group of followers, who told her she looked older post-facelift and needed a “hair transplant”. Then came the death threats. “I got a message that was... saying like, ‘die you f---ing slut’. Just terrible stuff,” she said. “You just think, ‘wow,’ but it says more about those people than it does about anyone else.”

McGinniss is happy with the result of her surgery and said she’d had minimal complications. Joanne McGinniss is happy with the results of her surgery and says she had minimal complications. But not all are so lucky. One Australian woman recently documented her physically gruelling recovery from a hotel room in Turkey after having a facelift, which left her skin puckered and her eyes cat-like, grotesque and asymmetrical. “You just have to trust the process,” she told her tens of thousands of followers. “Trust the process” is a common phrase used by those documenting their stories online, and positing videos of themselves at airports and waking up in hospital beds hooked up to plastic tubes. Sometimes, they film content with their beaming surgeons beside them; a way to promote the cosmetic clinics and receive discounted procedures.

title: Why Australia could be heading for a spring and summer 'triple whammy'
text:
In brief Climate change, a strong El Niño and another climate driver could combine forces this spring.

However, there are signs it's not all bad news for the summer bushfire threat.

Three climate forces are lining up ahead of spring, raising the odds of hotter and drier weather across parts of Australia.

The world is facing a potentially record-breaking El Niño, with the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) forecasting it will continue to intensify into a "very strong event" that may persist well into next year.

At the same time, another Australian climate driver associated with warmer and drier conditions — a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) — is expected to develop by spring.

"So, for Australia through the coming spring and summer, the double whammy of climate change and El Niño will be driving our weather. In actual fact, we might even have a triple whammy," Andrew Watkins, an adjunct professor at Monash University and a Climate Council researcher, told SBS News.

He said the IOD "is effectively El Niño but in the Indian Ocean".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Unfortunately, that pattern really sets in until summer, when the Asian monsoon comes in and knocks it over. But if we have climate change and El Niño and a positive Indian Ocean dipole, they are three things that all push south-east Australia into hotter and drier, and especially the spring period," he said.

Will Australia see a repeat of Europe's summer?

While an El Niño does not necessarily mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia, it does raise the likelihood.

As parts of Europe and the United States swelter through a summer of scorching heatwaves and fires, BoM climatologist Zhi-Weng Chua says soon, much of Australia will likely swelter too.

He says there is a high chance much of the nation's south-east and south-west will experience one of the warmest springs on record.

"Western parts of Western Australia, extending into southern Queensland and parts of south Australia, there is a strong indication that temperatures will be in the top 20 per cent of historical records for spring," he told SBS News.

But the heat expected during Australia's spring and summer are driven by different factors to those pushing temperatures skyward in Europe and North America.

Those continents have experienced the impact of climate change in the past few months, with record-high temperatures leading to high fire danger.

READ MORE How is climate change affecting El Niño and La Niña?

El Niño is an event measured by the sea surface temperature of the Pacific Ocean — it has a strong impact on the Asia Pacific, but far less on Europe and North America.

Sea surface temperatures in the central Pacific are now more than 2C above average — a level associated with a very strong El Niño — for the first time in a decade.

Australia's bushfire outlook

Greg Mullins is the former commissioner of Fire and Rescue NSW.

In recent years, he has used his expertise to drive action on climate change preparedness and risk evaluation, as a member of the Climate Council.

He recently told SBS News this year's converging climate drivers were extremely worrying, noting that emergency agencies were working with the BoM ahead of the release of the spring bushfire seasonal outlook, which would help guide preparations.

He said the combination of an El Niño with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole could drive "flash droughts" that heighten bushfire risk.

"Those two together can drive rapid drought, what we call flash drought, that you know within weeks you're suddenly in bad fire territory," he said.

"I know there's a lot of deep concern in all the fire agencies nationally," he said.

However, BoM meteorologists said there are signs that rain could disrupt the summer bushfire threat in many areas.

"That drier than average pattern that we're seeing for September does break down for much of the country and we start seeing either above average rainfall being favoured or even a not-clear signal for a lot of the country," Chua said.

Victoria and Tasmania, however, are expected to remain comparatively dry, he said.

title: Fast-tracked for Australian citizenship, this sports star has her sights set on LA 2028
text:
In brief Para taekwondo athlete Shrijana Ghising hopes to represent Australia at the 2028 Paralympics.

She was granted fast-tracked citizenship by the federal government.

Shrijana Ghising took up para taekwondo for fun when she was 18.

Eight years later, the 26-year-old is one of the world's top athletes in the sport and is chasing a place at the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles.

And as one of Australia's newest citizens, she hopes she will be wearing green and gold.

Originally from Nepal, Ghising won silver at the Gangwon-Chuncheon 2026 World Para Taekwondo Open Challenge in South Korea earlier this month — her first international tournament representing Australia.

"I'm so excited that now I am a citizen I can represent Australia in all the tournaments, but the big goal is LA28 … I want to be a medallist representing Australia," she said.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

She travelled to Australia on holiday in 2023 but quickly fell in love with the country.

"I have experienced a lot of discrimination in my life, but when I came to Australia everyone was very kind, and they did not treat me differently because of my disability," she said.

"Everyone in Australia is treated with the same respect.

Ghising won silver at the Gangwon-Chuncheon 2026 World Para Taekwondo Open Challenge in South Korea. Source: Supplied

"I love Australia, its culture and its people … I came for a holiday, but it became my home."

Ghising lived in Burnie, Tasmania, for two years before moving to Melbourne to further pursue her taekwondo career.

"My mother and my life partner motivated me to fulfil my taekwondo journey," she said.

Under special provisions of the Citizenship Act and with authorisation from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Ghising's citizenship application was expedited so she could compete for Australia at upcoming tournaments.

She officially became an Australian citizen at a ceremony in Melbourne's inner-west in June — just in time to represent Australia at the Para Taekwondo Open Challenge.

Australia has a special citizenship pathway for elite athletes and coaches to represent the country internationally.

The law was changed last year so Australian permanent residents who train or compete overseas as part of their sporting commitments are not disadvantaged in their pathway to citizenship, a move welcomed by the Australian Olympic Committee and Paralympics Australia.

However, refugee advocacy groups have previously said the rules should be broadened to include all people applying for Australian citizenship.

In 2009, when the government proposed shortening residency requirements for elite athletes, the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia welcomed the change but said it wanted everybody to be treated equally under citizenship law.

In 2024-25, a total of 165,193 people became Australian citizens, representing over 190 different nationalities.

Damien Kilner, from the Department of Home Affairs, said the federal government worked closely with sporting bodies to identify citizenship pathways for athletes seeking to represent Australia.

"Shrijana's journey from being a visitor who fell in love with this country to now preparing to represent the green and gold on the world stage highlights the important contributions new citizens can make to Australia and our international success," he said.

Ghising picked up para taekwondo for fun when she was a teenager. Source: Supplied

Paralympics Australia chief executive Cameron Murray welcomed Ghising to the Australian Paralympic movement.

"Para sport offers so much to Australians with disability, and it is pleasing that Shrijana is already experiencing its value, which can extend far beyond sport," he said.

"As part of our lead role within the Australian sporting system, Paralympics Australia looks forward to working with our partners to support Shrijana's journey as she strives to represent Australia on the international stage.

"Her story exemplifies the values that make our Paralympic movement so special: courage, resilience and the pursuit of opportunity."

title: What the upcoming nationwide e-bike crackdown means for you
text:
In brief New rules are set to come into place governing the use and capabilities of e-bikes.

The ACCC is drafting the new rules, which the government hopes will address safety issues.

A nationwide crackdown on high-speed e-bikes will seek to close regulatory loopholes after years of rising accidents and injuries, the federal government has announced.

On Thursday, Labor instructed the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to draft new standards for the sale of "e-micromobility" devices.

The new standards will apply to electric bikes, scooters and skateboards and are designed to prevent the sale of high-risk devices following a spike in e-bike injuries.

Assistant Competition Minister Andrew Leigh said the changes would inspire confidence in Australian consumers and send a clear message to industry.

"Nationally consistent standards will provide clearer expectations for manufacturers, retailers and consumers alike," he said.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What rules are currently in place for e-bikes?

Currently, regulatory enforcement varies between states and territories. Retailers can exploit the resultant loopholes to sell non-compliant devices.

Last year, Australia's state transport ministers agreed to mandate the international EN 15194 standard as the primary benchmark for e-bikes.

These standards restrict e-bikes to operating primarily through pedal assistance, cap their output, and require them to cut power once they reach 25km/h.

The new rules drafted by the ACCC will aim to close existing gaps after years of concerns over injuries and accidents, including from high-powered e-bikes.

The new consumer standards were proposed at a meeting of federal, state and territory consumer affairs ministers in Darwin in July.

Are the rules likely to be effective?

Harold Scruby, chief executive at the Pedestrian Council of Australia, said the announcement was a welcome step forward, but long overdue.

"It is too late," he told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

"Technology is always 10 years ahead of the law ... (but) we saw it coming."

Any changes must be complemented by consequences for retailers who fail to meet compliance standards, Scruby said.

Shared e-bike schemes have created a number of problems in many cities, but are used by many residents. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

"We've really got to clamp down on these cowboys who are selling these things to young children," he said.

Asked whether the horse had already bolted, Leigh insisted the changes complemented state-level crackdowns.

"There's work underway through transport ministers," he told Seven's Sunrise program on Thursday.

"This is about what can be sold."

Why are e-bikes so controversial?

E-bikes have been spruiked as an environmentally friendly, cost-affordable answer to congested city streets.

But the rollout of shared e-bike schemes — like Lime bikes and others — as well as their broader uptake across the nation have been clouded by rising injury and accident rates.

In 2024, NSW recorded 226 injuries related to e-bikes, which surged to 233 in the first seven months of 2025, including four deaths.

In Queensland, more than 6000 emergency department presentations were linked to e‑mobility devices between 2022 and 2025.

READ MORE Faulty e-bike battery sparks Sydney apartment evacuation

Queensland is among the states cracking down on illegal e-bikes, including with its police force's Operation Yankee Surety.

Some 249 illegal bikes were seized in the operation's first month following its launch on July 1, while riders were hit with 991 traffic infringement notices.

NSW Police and transport officers were in June granted powers to seize illegal e-bikes, to be pulverised by Transport for NSW.

Both states have been undertaking sweeping reforms of the electronic transport devices, but measures announced today will be the first nationwide effort to reform their use.

When will the new rules come into effect?

Work on the ACCC new e-micromobility standard is already underway.

Further details on enforcement timelines are unlikely to be released until consultation can be carried out with industry bodies and state regulators.

title: 'Don't bank on it': Three factors shaping next week's interest rates decision
text:
in brief The Reserve Bank board will decide on Tuesday whether to leave the cash rate at 4.35 per cent or change it.

Inflation, unemployment and household spending are three key economic indicators shaping the decision.

Millions of borrowers will be watching closely when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) announces its latest interest rates decision next week.

A mortgage expert says it will be a close call despite expectations among the 'big four' banks — Commonwealth Bank, Westpac, NAB and ANZ — that the central bank will leave the cash rate on hold at 4.35 per cent.

The RBA has already lifted rates three times this year, while governor Michele Bullock has refused to rule out further hikes as inflation remains above its 2-3 per cent target band.

"They've got a clock ticking in the background, particularly when it comes to inflation," said Sally Tindall, the data insights director at Canstar.

"The RBA board has repeatedly said that time is a factor in this battle with inflation because the longer we take to get back down, the harder it becomes, and the more entrenched inflation becomes".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The board will examine three key economic indicators released in recent weeks before handing down its decision on Tuesday.

Inflationary pressures

Inflationary pressures, as measured by both the consumer price index (CPI) and trimmed mean inflation, are frequently cited in the RBA's statements on its decision-making.

In June, the RBA said inflation was still too high and warned higher fuel and commodity costs are starting to flow into other parts of the economy, including housing and construction.

Bullock said Australia already had an inflation problem before disruptions to global oil markets caused by conflict in the Middle East.

The most recent data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) showed a shift in inflation in June.

Headline inflation fell from 4 per cent to 3.8 per cent while the trimmed mean, which strips out volatile items, remained steady at 3.6 per cent.

Source: SBS News

Tindall said that inflation predictions have shifted over time primarily due to the war in the Middle East, which has added to inflationary pressures.

The figures for June were "perhaps better than we were expecting," Tindall said, "but still a long way from target".

Source: SBS News

The RBA aims to bring inflation down to between 2 and 3 per cent, fulfilling one of its mandates to keep it low and stable.

Its other mandate is to support full employment, meaning as many Australians in work as possible without creating excessive inflation.

Unemployment rate

Tindall described the unemployment rate as "a critical data set for the RBA".

In June, the unemployment rate was 4.4 per cent, slightly below the 2026 peak of 4.5 per cent in April.

Source: SBS News

These figures have been on the RBA governor's mind. Earlier this month, Bullock said they were higher than expected.

However, Tindall said that while elevated, this figure of 4.4 per cent in itself is not going to push the board into "ringing an alarm bell".

Consumer spending

The amount households spend can give a sense of the average Australian's disposable income after they've made their mortgage payments.

This indicator gives the RBA a window into how households are faring amid economic pressures, including cost of living and the impact of higher interest rates.

READ MORE Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold

However, Tindall said this data can be hard to interpret.

"It's difficult to isolate in this data the families that are doing it incredibly tough versus the ones that aren't really sweating from the economic pressures at the moment," she said.

In June 2026, household spending rose 0.8 per cent month-on-month.

"Going further back with this data set, it's actually quite volatile, and there have been rises in June and May but a fall in April," Tindall said.

"The RBA will be paying attention to this, but will also look at other data points, including liaison programs, to better understand how Australian families are going."

Source: SBS News

Under these liaison programs, RBA economists consult with hundreds of private firms, industry associations, government agencies, and community organisations across Australia.

'Don't bank on it'

While the big four banks expect the RBA to leave rates unchanged on Tuesday, Tindall said borrowers should still be prepared for the possibility of another rate rise.

"I would say if you've got a mortgage, don't bank on it. Spend the weekend just going over your finances, making sure that you can withstand another rate hike. It might not happen on Tuesday, but it could still happen in the future," she said.

The big four banks predict the RBA won't move on rates until next year, when it will likely make its first cut since August 2025.

But that could change should overseas conflict escalate and put pressure on essential products like oil.

"Go out there and see if you can potentially get yourself a better deal with your bank," Tindall said.

"You can use the interest rate uncertainty as ammunition to negotiate with your own bank, or you could end up ultimately refinancing.

"But if you can get your own personalised rate cut, that will help future-proof your finances should we see another rate hike."

title: When to see a GP, visit urgent care or go to the emergency department this winter
text:
In Brief The Australian government has outlined three broad categories of care, each with varying symptom severity.

Chronic heart conditions, lung conditions, metabolic conditions, diabetes and kidney problems can all contribute to a worsening illness.

Getting the help you need for a winter illness could be simpler than spending hours waiting to be seen in a busy hospital emergency room.

That's the message the government is sending this flu season, a time when experts say hospitals tend to be the busiest, and wait times blow out.

While managing cold and flu cases is a national health concern, one state is taking a particularly strong stance, urging people to avoid the emergency room unless their lives are at risk.

On Monday, just under 10,000 people presented to emergency departments in Sydney, which the NSW health minister has described as the "biggest ever recorded winter day in history".

Professor Paul Griffin from the University of Queensland School of Medicine told SBS News that while numbers will vary between states, this time of year is often busy nationwide.

Across Australia, Griffin said healthcare services were seeing presentations of flu and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), as well as an increase in COVID-19 cases.

While these can be concerning conditions, an emergency room will always prioritise the most severe health conditions first, Griffin explained.

"If you don't need to go to your emergency department, it does free up valuable resources for them to be able to deal with more emerging cases," he said.

"There are a number of viable options for people that have conditions that are a little bit less urgent, and that's why we want people to make sure that they understand where the best place for them to go really is."

Where should you go?

It can depend on your symptoms and any underlying health conditions.

The Australian government has outlined three broad categories of care — routine, urgent and emergency — each with varying symptom severity, encompassing flu symptoms as well as broader conditions.

Most health issues can be addressed through routine care, which for many people means their GP.

Griffin said GPs are not only a good touchpoint for receiving care when sick but can also help you prepare a plan ahead of potential illness.

They can provide health checks, vaccinations and offer family and individual health advice.

"If it's something that you're not feeling needs urgent attention, then your GP is often the best place to start to get the care that you need," Griffin said.

Source: SBS News

If you start experiencing symptoms like chest pain or feel like a respiratory illness is worsening, you may want to consider going to an urgent care clinic (UCC) or the hospital.

"If you're breathing okay, even drinking okay, not systemically unwell, your GP is a really good place to start. If any of those things aren't the case, then I'd have a very low threshold for presenting to hospital," Griffin said.

"Whereas those urgent care clinics are really good for handling things that aren't imminently life-threatening and unlikely to require an admission to hospital."

Since 2023, the government has launched 137 urgent care clinics across the country.

"Medicare UCCs help reduce pressure on our hospitals and emergency departments, allowing them to focus on higher urgency and life-threatening conditions," a spokesperson for the Department of Health told SBS News.

Considerations for vulnerable Australians

Groups of people who are at highest risk for severe disease with respiratory viruses are Australians at the extremes of age: young children and older adults.

Griffin said that people who also have other medical conditions can be at further risk of illness.

"If you have a number of medical problems and you're an older adult and you get one of these respiratory viruses, it can certainly fairly rapidly progress to severe disease," he said.

Chronic heart conditions, lung conditions, metabolic conditions, diabetes and kidney problems can all contribute to a worsening illness.

"So understanding that risk, being proactive in having seen your GP or specialist before and having a plan is a really good way of managing the winter," Griffin said.

If you're not sure what kind of care is best for you, Griffin advised contacting a service such as Queensland's 13 HEALTH hotline or an after-hours GP for advice on the best escalation plan at the time.

The Australian government — through its free 1800MEDICARE service — also provides 24/7 health advice from registered nurses and connection to the right care, such as your regular GP, the local hospital or a Medicare UCC.

"In the after-hours period, and if clinically appropriate, callers may be offered a phone or video consultation with a 1800MEDICARE GP," the health department spokesperson said.

Not too late to act

Griffin said planning ahead with your GP is a great way to prepare for the winter flu season, as navigating complicated health services when you're sick can feel like an insurmountable task.

It's also not too late to vaccinate against common viruses.

"That includes influenza, and everyone should have one of those every year," Griffin said.

"For COVID, if you're high risk, it's probably every six to 12 months. But most people should get a COVID-19 vaccine once a year.

"And now with RSV vaccines being available, I'd certainly encourage anyone over 50 with medical problems or everyone over 70 to have had an RSV vaccine."

title: Kmart’s $89 glasses can record what you see. But what happens next?
text:
IN BRIEF AI smart glasses can record videos, make calls and translate speech or text in real time.

But experts have cautioned that the technology can be misused for dangerous or prohibited activity.

Kmart recently launched a new accessory — dubbed Camera Glasses — which it said blends stylish eyewear with built-in camera technology.

At a glance, the black-framed spectacles from Kmart's in-house brand Anko look like any ordinary pair of glasses. But by Monday 3 August, there were reports the product was sold out online.

At $89, the glasses provide a low-cost alternative to the smart glasses designed by glasses company Ray-Ban and Facebook owners Meta, which start at $337. The latest generation of this technology costs more than $700.

A recent promotional video for Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, featuring celebrity Kylie Jenner, showcased its features. Those include an ultra-HD camera, discreet open-ear Bluetooth speakers, and translation technology.

In July, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said people who don't wear smart glasses in the future will be at a "pretty significant cognitive disadvantage".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

There are similar products available or in development by the companies Samsung, Rokid, Even Realities, Solos and XREAL.

Milica Stilinovic is a postdoctoral research associate for the Governing Immersive Tech Project at the University of Sydney. She told SBS News that "a lot of flak has been driven towards Meta currently because they are market leaders".

Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses are available in a variety of colours and styles, including slim oval glasses designed by celebrity Kylie Jenner. Source: AP / Godofredo A Vásquez

But she said: "If the price is cheaper ... if you're not paying at the bridge, you may pay at the toll.

"We still need to ask ourselves, this data that we're essentially generating for these companies; how is it being handled, by whom and at what cost?"

Stilinovic also said wearable technology, regardless of its price point, raises complex questions around privacy and security.

'Computers for your face'

Put simply, Stilinovic said smart glasses are "computers for your face".

Depending on the product, they may have AI-enabled programs embedded, which analyse human behaviours including eye movements, head tracking and voice patterns.

"They are picking up data of where you're walking around, the space that you're in, what you're doing at particular times ... even to the extent of knowing the map out of your home," Stilinovic said.

Facial recognition technology is not active in most smart glasses on the market.

However, in 2024, students from Harvard University combined smart glasses, facial search engines, AI language tools and public databases to test surveillance capabilities. They found information including a person's home address, name and phone number — just by looking at them.

Fareed Kaviani is a research fellow at the Emerging Technologies Research Lab at Monash University. In 2024, he co-authored a paper examining social perceptions of smart glasses use in Australia.

Of more than 1,000 Australians surveyed, 13.5 per cent of smart glasses owners admitted to dangerous usage like wearing the technology while driving or cycling. Around 17 per cent of people admitted to prohibited use, including antisocial behaviour or recording people without consent.

Kaviani told SBS News this research was conducted in 2022, "when the device was not as well known and ubiquitous as it probably is today".

He also said his research relied on self-reported data: "The real prevalence of dangerous or prohibitive use is difficult to establish. It could be higher, it could be lower."

He found that younger people in Australia were more likely to own the glasses, but age safeguards around the technology were not always clear.

What does the law say?

Avinash Singh, principal lawyer at Astor Legal, told SBS News he believes most people have "no clue" about the laws regarding cameras or smart glasses.

The Australian Privacy Principles, which govern standards, rights and obligations around the collection and use of personal information, are considered "technology-neutral" and can adapt to changing technologies, according to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.

This means smart glasses are governed at state and territory levels.

In Australia, it is a criminal offence to film a person in a private or intimate circumstance like a bathroom or change room without consent.

Singh prefaced that "private conversations don't necessarily have to be in a private space".

"They can just be two people or more than two people speaking in public. But, if there's an inference that the people having that conversation would expect that to remain a private conversation — that will satisfy the definition."

In most states and territories, there are also distinctions between audio and video recording laws. Source: AP / Jack Dempsey

He also told SBS News that in most parts of Australia, if a person is recording in public using smart glasses without informing people they're filming, "they would be committing an offence".

Queensland is an exception. People can record a conversation without the other party knowing as long as they are a participant in the conversation.

If an offence is committed, Singh said individuals, not companies, will be responsible.

"In the same way as if someone went out, took a hammer and committed an assault, the manufacturer of the hammer would not be held responsible."

'Murkier waters'

If a person uses wearable technology to repeatedly target or intimidate a person, the user may breach stalking and harassment laws.

Additional legal issues can also arise when recordings are shared publicly online, including doxing and online misuse.

Singh believes that Australian privacy laws were drafted when there was no anticipation this technology would become prominent:

"The current legal framework never envisioned that you would be able to wear a pair of glasses and record people without them knowing what was happening," he said.

"I think more significant for a lot of people is ... sharing it online and people effectively making a commercial gain from criminal offences."

Stilinovic has also analysed social media videos captured using smart glasses. She found recordings ranged from advertorial content to the "murkier waters of pickup artists" which often form part of the online manosphere.

She believes state laws can be "fragmented" and called for additional enforcement.

"For too long, we're dealing with a situation in which technology is unleashed onto society, and we don't have the guardrails in place. Then, the harm happens, and then regulators have to scramble to try to protect us from that harm."

title: 'Not a lot of time for nerves': At a Greek airbase, this Australian is waiting for a call
text:
IN BRIEF A small but growing number of Australian private aerial firefighting companies are now based in Europe every summer.

Pilot Alex Pay from the NSW Hunter says his community in Greece are welcoming and appreciative of their work.

While most Australians in Europe are at the beach, NSW aerial firefighting pilot Alex Pay spends his long summer days at a Greek airbase, waiting for a call to action.

"When you get a fire call, you're gonna be airborne in 15 minutes," he told SBS News.

"So there's not a lot of time for nerves."

Once in the air, Pay can spend up to 10 hours supporting local authorities in Greece's fight against wildfires, which over the past week saw two pilots killed and hundreds of thousands forced to evacuate.

Pay, 31, works for a small but growing number of Australian private aerial firefighting companies based in Western Europe during this year's fire season, which is shaping up to be the continent's worst in record.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It also comes as Australia's own looming El Niño threatens to turn up the heat on our own summer bushfire risk.

The 'Fire Boss'

Pay is a third-generation pilot with Pay's Air Service, which is based in the NSW Hunter Region.

"I remember as a kid flying with my dad to visit my grandparents," he told SBS News.

He pilots one of 14 aircraft his company has based throughout Greece for the summer. It’s his second season in the country, and the fifth overall for his company.

"The biggest thing is that we don't try to take risks," he said.

They fly a variant of the Air Tractor AT-802, nicknamed the "Fire Boss" — an amphibious aircraft that scoops water into a tank, or "hopper", controlled by a computerised fire gate that can be adjusted to match exact conditions.

Australian aerial firefighting companies are increasingly supporting European ground crews when it comes to tackling climate-change induced fires. Source: Supplied / Chris Boyd/Aerotech Aviation

In Australia, there were around 130 certified firefighting aeroplane operators or individual pilots, with a further 186 helicopter operators in 2021, according to Australia's Civil Aviation Authority.

Andrew Mackay is from Ballarat-based Field Air Group, which also has planes stationed in Greece this summer supporting Pay's.

"We like to say in our industry that it's not the aircraft that put out the fires, it's the ground crew — we're merely a tool to assist them," he told SBS News.

He said pilots will often work on either side of the fire to create a "triangle or an arrowhead, so the fire comes to a point where the ground crew can then extinguish that".

Sometimes they will drop water or retardant directly onto a house under threat from a blaze.

"We spent a lot of time training and preparing scenarios that give us a good education on what we might see on the fire ground," Pay said.

One of Pay's amphibious Fire Boss aircraft. Source: Supplied / Pay's Air Service

Despite stringent safety procedures, accidents can still occur.

On Sunday, a Greek and a Danish national were killed after two helicopters collided while fighting a fire west of Athens.

The helicopters were leased from Australian company McDermott Aviation, which said in a statement it was "deeply saddened" by the tragedy.

In Australia, there were 32 aerial firefighting accidents between 2000 and 2023, causing six fatalities, according to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau.

'Hotter and drier than usual'

In Bordeaux, where tens of thousands of people were evacuated in recent wildfires , local authorities were supported by Adelaide-based Aerotech Group, which has four aircraft, six pilots and a ground crew in the southern French city.

It's their fourth year working in Bordeaux, and according to CEO Chris Boyd, the "most intense" to date.

"Basically, from the beginning of the season, it’s been busy … It's been hotter and drier than usual, and they've still got a lot more of the fire season to go," Boyd said.

An AT-802, or "Fire Boss", sits on the tarmac. Source: Supplied / Chris Boyd/Aereotech Aviation

Like Pay’s, Aerotech started in agricultural aviation spraying crops, but these days 80 per cent of the company's work is in aerial firefighting — across Australia, Europe and Indonesia.

"The need for firefighting isn't going away," Boyd said.

He said the demand for Australian aerial firefighting in the northern hemisphere is driven by intensifying fire seasons in Europe.

Europe is warming faster than the rest of the world, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service's European State of the Climate Report, which estimates the continent is warming by 0.56C per decade more than the global average.

Last year, 95 per cent of Europe saw above-average temperatures.

Another contributing factor is Europe's urban sprawl.

"We have more people out in the rural interface in areas that once upon a time ... would have burned and not been a problem," Boyd said.

'Happy to be here'

Former commissioner of Fire and Rescue NSW, Greg Mullins, said aerial firefighting is a "useful tool" but not without its challenges, especially as climate change makes fires more unpredictable.

"The textbooks are constantly being rewritten on fire behaviour," Mullins said.

Aerial firefighting aircraft can only fly during the day and are grounded during pyro-convective storms — when fires are so "intense they push up into the stratosphere and form a storm cloud from the smoke column".

"Every aircraft has to land because they are being knocked out of the sky," he said.

Alex's six month-old daughter is a hit with the local community. Source: Supplied / Alex Pay

Still, Mullins said there's nothing quite like the sight of an aeroplane or helicopter when you're on the ground fighting a fire.

"When they come overhead, you go, 'Thank God!'" he said.

Despite the challenges, Pay said he loves being up in the air and "the freedom it brings with it".

This season, Pay brought his wife and six-month-old daughter to stay with him in Greece, where he said his baby "is a hit" with the locals — especially the older generation.

"A lot of them would love her first word to be something Greek."

He said the local community are welcoming and often get to know the pilots as they return each year, bringing them food and inviting them to barbecues.

"When they realise what we're here to do, they're very appreciative and they're always coming up and saying thank you," Pay said.

"We're just happy to be here."

title: Jetstar’s new overhead baggage rules explained: When they start and what you'll pay
text:
In brief Jetstar will charge between $25 and $52 for carry-on bags stored in overhead lockers from February 2027.

New size-based baggage rules scrap routine weighing and offer priority boarding for paying travellers.

Storing carry-on baggage in overhead lockers on Jetstar flights will cost up to $52 one-way, as the budget airline announces new charges for passengers.

Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully says the changes to the airline's carry-on baggage allowances will streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time.

"Our new carry-on baggage model provides more choice to customers while helping to keep our fares low," Tully added.

"You only pay for what you need — travelling with less means paying less, and you can always add more if you need."

The changes follow "extensive research and feedback from customers and crew" which found frustrations with weighing bags and finding enough room in overhead lockers, Jetstar said.

What's changing and what you'll pay now

From 2 February, Jetstar will lift its 7kg carry-on weight limit in favour of a size-based carry-on baggage model.

Cabin baggage scales used to weigh passengers' carry-on bags before boarding will no longer be "routinely" used, the airline said.

Passengers will be able to bring one small bag to place under the seat, such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag. That bag can weigh up to 10kg and be up to 40 x 30 x 20cm. Any bags larger than that will incur a fee.

title: A growing number of children are falling behind at school. Here's what the data shows
text:
In brief One in three students missed basic NAPLAN benchmarks as reading scores fell across all year levels.

Families of children needing extra support say results can be demoralising.

Ruby and her 11-year-old son Mark were dreading the day his scores on the national school assessment program were released.

And they confirmed the family's worst fears: despite working hard to learn, the Year 5 student remained behind his peers.

Mark, whose name the Australian Associated Press agreed not to publish, was one of more than 1.3 million children in Years 3, 5, 7, and 9 who sat the National Assessment Program — Literacy and Numeracy (NAPLAN) in 2026.

As the only standardised national assessment, NAPLAN was primarily designed to help governments and schools measure results and fix funding or teaching shortfalls.

But for students such as Mark, seeing their results can be demoralising.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He has ADHD and autism and needs extra support at school.

"When I got the results, because it comes under Mark's name, he wanted to see his results,'' Ruby said.

"In his reading column ... it actually said the bottom, bottom.

"I just thought to myself, 'How could it be right at the bottom when he's improved so much?'"

READ MORE Pioneering Australian school aims to prove there's more to education than NAPLAN

But scores for reading were worse than in 2025 for every year level, and Year 5 students were the only cohort whose writing ability had improved.

Overall, about one in three students across all levels did not meet basic literacy and numeracy benchmarks, falling into "developing" and "needs additional support" categories.

The writing scores were a particular concern in the two lowest grades tested, with less than 10 per cent of students exceeding national benchmarks.

Numeracy results had improved for most cohorts since 2025, though Year 3's score had decreased.

Results from previous years showed a clear literacy divide between children from wealthy, educated areas and those who grow up in areas of low socio-economic status.

Ruby said she also struggled at school and her challenges went unnoticed because of her learning environment.

She is now raising her children on a low income.

"With Mark, I just wish there was more people, just more at the school to help," she said.

Better support that understands the specific needs of struggling families would help improve results, The Smith Family chief executive Doug Taylor said.

"With 72,000 low-income students across Australia, the right support at the right time can make a huge difference," he said, noting schools should also consider the skills students had beyond academic ones.

In rural communities and towns with high Indigenous populations, results have dramatically improved in recent years.

That was due to increased funding and the use of explicit teaching models, Education Minister Jason Clare said in a speech at the Garma Indigenous festival over the weekend.

"Over the last four years, the numeracy results of Indigenous students have gone up and up,'' he said.

"In Year 5 by 9.5 points and in Year 7 by 9.3 points. That's a good sign."

Separately, the federal government's commitment to cover a quarter of the Schooling Resource Standard to reach full funding for public schools was rolled out in 2026.

In October, the controversial Thriving Kids program will, in part, replace the National Disability Insurance Scheme for children under nine with development delays.

Tasmanian students did not sit NAPLAN in 2026 because of industrial action.

title: 2026 Census: The new questions on gender and sexual orientation explained
text:
IN BRIEF Two new questions have been added to the Census about gender identity and sexual orientation.

A question on ancestry has been expanded to allow up to four responses.

The Census of Population and Housing has long tracked a changing Australia — but for more than a century, a piece of the nation's story has been missing, LGBTIQ+ Health Australia CEO Nicky Bath says.

Bath says the organisation has been calling for the addition of questions regarding sexual orientation, gender identification and expression.

"I remember in the run-up to the 2021 Census being contacted by older people who thought that they wouldn't be alive for the 2026 Census, and it was very sad for them that they wouldn't be able to participate ... in this way," she told SBS News.

What are the new Census questions?

The 2026 Census will now include two new questions about gender and sexual orientation.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Respondents will still be asked about their sex recorded at birth, but people over the age of 16 can also specify their gender as male, female, non-binary or another term.

An optional question regarding sexual orientation has been added, with answers including straight, gay or lesbian, bisexual or an open-ended response for another term.

Why is the Census collecting this information?

Bath said Census data — which will be released in three phases starting from June 2027 — will inform the availability, funding and location of LGBTQI+ community and health services.

If people in Australia do not complete the Census they can be fined up to $364 a day. Credit: ABS

"The decision has been a long time coming ... for many people, being able to mark those boxes in the Census is really important with regards to validation and for us to be seen as important members of the community. That's a really important historical moment."

What wasn't included in the new questions?

Advocates like Equality Australia say the number of people living in houseboats has been recorded in the Census for decades, but LGBTQI+ populations have not been traced.

Anna Brown, CEO of Equality Australia, said Census data collected about LGBTQI+ people would be "transformative".

"We're really looking forward to learning just how many LGBTQ+ people there are in Australia, because we know that if we aren't counted, we remain invisible in the data that shapes decisions about our lives," she told SBS News.

"Better data leads to better decisions on health, housing, education, aged care, and community services. Until now, governments have been making these decisions without a complete picture of our communities."

Brown has also called for Australians with innate variations of sex characteristics or intersex people to be counted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

"We will continue to advocate for its inclusion and work with the ABS ... towards recommending that this population be included," she said.

Census questions are informed by the 2020 ABS standards for sex, gender, variations in sex characteristics, and sexual orientation variables. These standards specify that: "The inclusion of born with a variation of sex characteristics or intersex as a response option in a sex question ... is not capable of generating reliable or consistent results in measuring this population, and perpetuates the misconception that intersex people are neither male nor female."

Bath said more work is needed to ensure Australians are educated about innate variations of sex characteristics, which she believes is often "conflated with sex and gender".

However, she is choosing to view Census outcomes with a glass "half full" approach.

READ MORE Agency behind Australian census admits there was a problem with 'non-binary' question

"We know that there are challenges with not having the gender question being asked to people who are under 16. That means that people with trans and gender diverse children are not going to be able to inform the Census about their children.

"On the other side of that, though, we will get data for the first time on people who are over 16, and that is very, very important," Brown said.

What else has changed in the 2026 Census?

Jenny Telford, general manager of the Census and Population division at the ABS, said answers have also been expanded to reflect the "rich cultural makeup across the country".

Previously, an ancestry question, which gathered data on people's lineage or descent, only allowed up to two response options. Now, respondents can provide up to four answers.

Telford said the change will provide "richer insights into the cultural makeup of every area across Australia".

Jenny Telford, general manager of the Census and Population division at the ABS, said the Census provides critical data on "who we are and how we are changing over time". Credit: ABS

Peter Doukas is the chair of the Federation of Ethnic Communities Councils of Australia, the peak body representing Australians from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.

"We were very much in support of the ancestry data being added to [the Census] and I think we're going to see some very interesting results in terms of not only people from a non-English-speaking or cultural background, but also from First Nations backgrounds," he told SBS News.

The ABS has announced it aims to better reflect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural identity.

"So getting a good count of our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander population in the 2026 Census is a really important priority for the ABS," Telford said.

"We've expanded things like the languages that people can report on the Census form to include more Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages than we've had in the past."

On 11 August, the ABS will also ask people how they travelled to work. The Census has updated its response category to include a new bicycle option (including e-bike) to reflect what it described as "more contemporary modes of travel".

title: As allies desert FIFA boss Gianni Infantino, is there anyone ready to replace him?
text:
In brief Key allies continue to turn on FIFA president Gianni Infantino.

His plan to privatise parts of the World Cup has exploded into one of football's biggest controversies in years.

Pressure on FIFA president Gianni Infantino has intensified, with opposition emerging both within world football's governing body and from external critics over his since-abandoned proposal to open the World Cup to private investment.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, appointed in 2019 by Infantino as FIFA's chief of global football development, said in a statement on Tuesday that "the decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question".

His remarks followed hot on the heels of an extraordinary internal email to FIFA staff, seen by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency, in which secretary-general Mattias Grafstrom appeared to distance himself from Infantino on the issue.

Previously seen as close to Infantino, Grafstrom describes the fiasco surrounding the plan as "a sad and reproachable series of events".

FIFA floated the plan last Tuesday, saying it could raise up to US$4.2 billion ($5.95 billion) of private investment based on a valuation of US$20 billion ($28 billion) for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would handle commercial rights for events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

By Saturday, it was dead in the water, as Infantino announced he was abandoning the plan after widespread condemnation, with European governing body UEFA having threatened to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.

Far from calming the waters or shoring up his presidency, Infantino has been swamped with criticism of his leadership style; the previously smooth path to being re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term next March now looks rocky.

'Take immediate steps'

However, re-election is a problem down the road. For now, Infantion has others to confront.

Even though he had withdrawn the scheme, UEFA issued a letter through their lawyers in the US threatening legal action over what they had scathingly described as a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal".
