"You and FIFA are required to take immediate steps to identify, locate, and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this Notice that are in your or FIFA's possession, custody, or control," its lawyer Andrew Levander said in the letter sent last Friday and seen by AFP.

Several of UEFA's member associations — Wales, Finland, Sweden and Serbia — have withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino and the English FA is strongly rumoured to be on the verge of joining them.

The scant comfort for Infantino came from a handful of supporters, including 2030 World Cup co-hosts Morocco, along with Kuwait, Qatar, where he has a house, and Lebanon, which granted him honorary citizenship in February.

The criticism only adds to the impression that Infantino has lost the confidence of even his closest FIFA collaborators.

A new challenger approaches?

Among Infantino's detractors, the hunt for a replacement has reportedly already begun.

The question now is whether his opposition can rally round one candidate with the deadline for nominations arriving on 18 November.

The name most frequently mentioned as a potential challenger or successor is Victor Montagliani, president of CONCACAF, which governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean.

READ MORE The $28 billion plan at the centre of a growing FIFA storm

An emboldened opposition could also move sooner than that and call for an emergency meeting of the FIFA Council.

That would require the backing of 19 of the 37 members of the FIFA Council, triggering a meeting that must be held within two weeks.

In theory, the opposition has the numbers to force such a meeting, as the three confederations who were scathing of Infantino's leadership control 21 seats on the council.

European football's governing body UEFA has nine members, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has seven, while CONCACAF boasts five.

There is another more radical option, but one that is conceivable given the backlash: a no-confidence vote in Infantino.

An extraordinary FIFA congress can be held if 20 per cent of the 211 member associations formally request it in writing.

It would take the support of just 43 member associations to spark such a move, a threshold that could easily be assembled from UEFA (55 members), CONCACAF (35) and AFC (46).

Should it come down to a leadership contest, Montagliani appears the obvious challenger as a non-European candidate. Europe has held the post since Sepp Blatter was elected in 1998.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin and Norway's football chief Lise Klaveness — who would be the first woman elected as president — have both ruled themselves out in the past.

title: Australians seeing record gains and losses, as 'cracks' in housing market appear
text:
Key Points A smaller number of properties made a profit in the first half of 2026 compared to 12 months prior.

Some areas experienced records gains and losses from property sales.

Property prices in Australia consistently reach record highs, but a "first crack in profitability" could signal a market downturn.

In the first half of 2026, 97.4 per cent of house resales resulted in a profit, slightly down from 97.5 per cent 12 months prior, according to new data from Domain released on Wednesday.

While it is a modest decline of just 0.1 per cent, it may indicate that the extended period of strong resale profitability is beginning to taper off.

Most people selling properties will still make "substantial gains", Domains chief residential economist Nicola Powell told SBS News.

However, the slight fall in national profitability suggests a slowing property market that could see prices fall in the future.

"While that shift is small, I think it is significant because what it's telling us is that resale profitability is a lagging indicator and tends to follow changes in home pricing," she explained.

"We've got some of our capital cities now going backward in price and particularly in some of our markets, we are seeing an increase in loss-making resales."

Source: SBS News

REA Group Senior Economic Analyst Megan Lieu said realestate.com.au data also revealed a drop in profitability.

In the past six months to July, 94.4 per cent of home resales made a profit, down from 94.9 per cent in the previous six months to January, she said.

But while properties are seeing larger average losses as profitability declines, some markets are soaring.

Where are people making and losing money on property?

While slightly fewer properties are making a profit compared to 12 months ago, successful sellers are still enjoying record returns.

Median resale profits climbed to record levels of $458,000 for houses and $237,000 for units nationally.

In the capital cities, median house profits were even higher at $552,000.

Sydney posted the country’s largest resale returns, with the median house vendor achieving a profit of $739,500.

Meanwhile, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide are increasingly standing out as the strongest markets for seller returns, with almost every resale delivering a gain.

Source: SBS News

Perth recorded the greatest proportion of profitable house resales, with 99.6 per cent of sellers making a profit on their transaction. Brisbane led the unit market, where 99.5 per cent of resales generated a positive return.

In contrast, Melbourne remained the weakest capital city market for units. More than one in four sellers sold for less than their original purchase price, while Melbourne also recorded one of the highest shares of loss-making house resales, alongside Canberra.

Surprisingly, some areas saw both record profitability gains and losses over the year.

READ MORE The growing constituency reshaping Australian politics

Powell explained that record-high losses come from a small pool of sales.

"Those losses are perhaps large because they're in financial strife," she said.

"Or perhaps they've maybe leveraged themselves too much; they've stretched themselves too much to keep up with voracious price gains."

Home values and sale volumes fall

As overall profitability has fallen, home values and the number of properties sold have declined, according to Cotality.

In its latest report released on Monday, the group found that home values had fallen by 0.7 per cent in July and fewer people had listed their properties.

Source: SBS News

Cotality Head of Research Gerard Burg said that nationally, total home listings sat 1.1 per cent below the five-year average over the four weeks ending 26 July.

"There remains a mismatch between the pricing expectations of buyers and sellers," Burg said in the report.

"Capital city auction clearance rates have remained below 50 per cent since late May, although they have moved up from the low 40s range in mid-to-late June."

Source: SBS News

Lieu said that higher interest rates and tax changes from the federal budget are also contributing to a market slowdown.

"We expect prices to fall further in 2026, however, the extent of the decline will depend on the trajectory of interest rates and supply," she said.

A growing divide

Looking at property markets across Australia shows a "growing divide" in prices that Powell expects will continue.

On the one hand, the largest property markets — Melbourne and Sydney — are seeing prices weaken, while smaller markets in Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane continue to soar.

Source: SBS News

"Both Melbourne and Sydney are seeing an uplift in housing supply, so that increase in housing stock is giving buyers more choice," Powell explained.

While those capitals could continue to fall in price, it could be some time before other cities hit a price ceiling.

Source: SBS News

Powell said these shifts in profits and losses are normal in the property market.

"Making money off of property is about being in it for the long game," she said.

"Staying put increases your chances of actually making a healthy profit upon reselling that home, because you're riding the waves and the turns that make up the property price cycle."

InspirationSweden Port guide: Visby, Sweden Brian Johnston August 7, 2026 — 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This article is part of Traveller’s ultimate guide to cruise ports. See all stories .

One of northern Europe’s best-preserved medieval towns is an absolute charmer, and sits over the horizon from the worst of the continent’s old-town tourist hordes. Who goes there Baltic cruises have become increasingly popular, and the cruise season has been steadily extended, with some ships now visiting even in winter. As a result, a wide variety of cruise lines visit Visby on Gotland, including Azamara, Celebrity, Cunard, Holland America, Lindblad Expeditions, Ponant, Princess and Scenic, among others. Cruises typically start and finish in Copenhagen or Stockholm, but sometimes further afield in Amsterdam or Southampton. Sail on in Almedalen Park in Visby. Swedish Tourism

Advertisement

The low-lying island of Gotland won’t provide much scenery from the Visby side, and nor will you see much of Visby’s fortifications and towers because (unusually) this medieval town doesn’t perch atop a hill. A huge silo on the headland will fool you into thinking it’s a castle for a while. In short, you won’t miss out on much if you’re intent on enjoying the breakfast buffet. Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now. Berth rites Ships dock at a plain concrete quay two kilometres from the old town. A small shed-like terminal is the only excitement, and you may not be in it if your ship ties up on the open quay. The bigger terminal with the bridge arms is for disembarking passengers off ferries from the Swedish mainland. You could walk into town in 30 minutes, but free shuttles are the better option. There isn’t much point in the hop-on hop-off bus, since it can’t enter the old town. Going ashore The former Hanseatic league trading port and World Heritage walled city, overlooked by 27 towers, is where you want to wander. Some of the fortifications and churches are in ruins, but medieval Visby is otherwise very well preserved. It’s more about the overall picture and atmosphere rather than any particular buildings, but the Cathedral of St. Mary and the ruined Dominican Monastery are worth a look. The very good Gotland Museum covers 5000 years of the island’s history, and exhibits prehistoric carved stones, Viking silver coins, medieval art and more.

Advertisement

Don’t miss UNESCO World Heritage Site the Visby City Wall, or Ringmuren. Swedish Tourism Amid all the medieval architecture and cobbled quaintness, it’s easy to miss the free DBW’s Botanical Garden, which were first laid out in the 19th century. Although small, the gardens are delightful and showcase roses and exotic trees. A gate leads through the city wall nearby and onto the waterfront. Get active You could walk around the base of the medieval walls, which run for 3.5 kilometres, or stick to the promenades that meander along the waterfront. If you want to get further along the coast and around parts of the island, rent a bicycle. Hogklint Nature Reserve just outside town is a good place for walking, with views from limestone cliffs. You can rock climb and abseil, mountain bike and horse ride elsewhere on Gotland.

Advertisement

Related Article Europe Europe’s most enjoyable old town has no crowds and no fees Best bites Seafood is naturally foremost on an island, and on Gotland particularly smoked salmon, herring (often accompanied by potatoes and a cream-based sauce) and pickled fish. However, Gotland lamb is dished up in hearty stews. In summer, cloudberries, dewberries and lingonberries are a must-try. The dish most associated with Visby is a saffron rice pancake served with cloudberry jam, and there’s no lack of cafés in which to enjoy it. Further afield Although Visby is the highlight, Gotland island has plenty more for the inquisitive visitor, including unusual boat-shaped Bronze Age graves, Viking history, pretty churches and villages such as fishing village Gnisvard, and surprisingly wild landscapes. A typical excursion will take you on an island overview. Some cruise lines offer a local farm experience with tastings of local produce or insight into wool textile making.

title: These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal
text:

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age August 7, 2026 — 12:54pm

August 7, 2026 — 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The AFL commission chairman Craig Drummond was president of Geelong, and part of the deliberations and ultimate decision, when the Cats struck what has been acknowledged was an inappropriate waiver with a player who had a history of concussions. On Thursday, as the story detonated that the Cats had signed the player to a waiver that diminished his legal rights – at least on paper – Drummond was asked to respond to questions from this masthead, and doubtless other media, about his role in the shonky waiver. Craig Drummond’s brief statement does not address the questions that need to be answered about the concussion waiver Geelong signed with a senior player when he was the club’s president. AFL Photos via Getty Images The AFL chairman, who holds the highest office in the game, issued a brief statement that did not address the obvious questions that he should have taken on, given his twin hats as AFL chairman and the president of the club at the time that this hubristic document was signed, without the AFL’s consent or knowledge. Drummond’s AFL chose not to sanction Geelong, a matter of months after Carlton was fined $75,000 for their handling of the Elijah Hollands affair, which was about a different kind of player safety – mental health.

Advertisement

The AFL took weeks to sort through the messy Hollands imbroglio before settling on a sanction. They needed only half a day to rule that the Cats were off the hook. Drummond’s time as AFL chairman has won praise within clubs for the energetic reshaping of the commission and introducing the kind of governance – term limits for the board, most of all – that were not evident during the Richard Goyder era, in which Gillon McLachlan was allowed to run his race. Loading But, as with political leaders, AFL honeymoons are as fleeting as Essendon winning streaks and Drummond did not last the whole 2026 season without finding himself in political cow manure. His statement contained the clichéd motherhood lines about the clubs and AFL continuing “to prioritise the health and safety of all our players”.

Advertisement

Those words read as utterly hollow, since Geelong had not made the player’s “health and safety” their priority in the now-recanted part of the agreement. The whole objective of the waiver was to absolve the club of responsibility for the player’s long-term health (in relation to head injuries) and put the onus on the player. The only excuse for the Cats is that it would have been easier to not offer him a contract (the AFL concussion panel had cleared him to play). While it was the player’s initiative that this deal be struck, the Cats went off the reservation by getting him to sign away legal protections. Before he became AFL chairman, Craig Drummond was Cats president, He’s pictured here in 2022 with star Patrick Dangerfield after the club won the 2022 grand final. Getty Carefully crafted statements, without answering questions, is a strategy that could succeed for Drummond and the AFL given society’s attention spans, which are shorter than the time it took the league to clear the Cats. Drummond, however, has a responsibility to address questions about an embarrassing, ill-considered and furtive arrangement that has not – to my knowledge – been tried on by other AFL clubs. If an oft-concussed player signed a waiver or its equivalent in the VFL, before he was drafted on to an AFL list, that still falls short of Geelong’s too-clever ploy.

Advertisement

Drummond was at the helm of Geelong when this happened, and holds even greater responsibility now as AFL chairman. These questions, which he hasn’t yet padded up for, should be answered candidly, in full: Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player As president of Geelong in 2024, does he take responsibility for the waiver the club signed with the player? Do he and Geelong owe the player an apology? Why was this waiver necessary? Did any parts trouble him then? You’ve called Geelong’s changes “appropriate.” Can you clarify if you regret that you were a party to this arrangement? You say health and safety of players is paramount. Why was Geelong not sanctioned, for an arrangement that went outside the AFL and the AFL Players Association, and which will be disallowed in future? Carlton was sanctioned with a $75,000 fine for allowing a medically unfit player on the field. Please explain the vast gap in consequence for Carlton’s offence and Geelong’s missteps? Given the conflict of interest between your roles as Geelong president then, and AFL chairman now, how did you ensure that the decisions and discussions within the AFL were not influenced by your interests? What steps, if any, did you take? This episode underscores that Geelong’s greatness as a footy club has little basis in some imagined moral superiority of “values” and decency; the narrative some ex-Geelong players and officials unwisely spruik. Yes, the Cats are exceptional – in coaching, recruiting and development, not in niceness, humility and tender care. They come across as a ruthless organisation that makes hard calls and is focused on winning games, not friends or wellbeing awards. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has lashed out at Channel Seven, claiming the broadcaster pulled out of funding her travel expenses in the UK, and denied reports in this masthead that she left luxury hotel rooms in London empty while she travelled to Italy. Hanson conceded on Friday a key claim, first reported in this masthead, that she used party funds to pay for a stay in a $900-a-night five-star hotel in London. The One Nation leader, who is ascendant in the polls, travelled to Europe on a 10-day “fact-finding” mission in July, during which she filmed a program with Seven’s Spotlight program. Hanson spoke at CPAC GB in London in July. Luca Marino During the trip Hanson sat down with far-right agitator and criminal Tommy Robinson, and appeared at CPAC GB, a conservative conference headlined by Nigel Farage. Hanson admitted in a Facebook post on Friday morning that she used the party’s money, rather than her own funds, to pay for the luxury accommodation, but denied she had left rooms empty in London during a trip to Italy to meet mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.

The One Nation leader claimed that Seven pulled out of paying for the UK trip, obliging her to use party funds. Related Article Exclusive

Political expenses Empty five-star room: Hanson paid for $900-a-night hotel with party funds “Spotlight have been shady from day one. Original travel plans for the Spotlight episode were to be paid by Channel Seven. They pulled out forcing One Nation to cover all travel costs,” Hanson wrote. A spokesperson for Channel Seven said the broadcaster did not pay for any travel expenses for One Nation. “Seven paid for incidentals, including a vehicle used in the production process and a hotel room used for filming purposes as well as security to protect Seven staff while recording on UK streets, but no travel expenses for One Nation.”

Hanson’s attacks on Seven and this masthead cap off a week in which she on Monday barred The Age, the ABC and The Guardian from a Melbourne press conference where the party announced eight candidates for the November state election. Stating that “mainstream media publish lies”, Hanson wrote that she provided Expedia invoices to news.com.au journalist Samantha Maiden to prove she cancelled her London accommodation while in Italy. News.com.au reported Hanson had used interest generated from a $20 million donation pot to pay for the accommodation. A screenshot of a partial invoice published by the outlet appears to show five days’ accommodation at the Conrad Saint James Hilton from July 15. Hanson’s declaration of interests shows Rinehart paid for flights from London to Sicily via Rome on July 11 and return on July 16. The screenshot does not include the hotel name, Expedia branding, or the date the booking was made. It is also only for one room, not for the other staff who stayed at the time. “I can confirm that while I was in Italy, accommodation in London was cancelled,” Hanson said on Facebook. A source familiar with the trip told this masthead earlier this week Hanson left rooms vacant at the luxury London for days while she was in Italy with Rinehart, where she attended a Dolce and Gabbana fashion show.

Another source suggested the lavish trip had caused unease within One Nation because it was sitting on a fresh $5 million war chest from the viral Fire the Liar fundraising campaign, which had bolstered the party’s coffers off the back of ordinary Australians chipping in small amounts to campaign against Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. This masthead sent questions to One Nation over several days about the London accommodation. One Nation did not answer the questions or provide invoices, and only stated that the Fire the Liar campaign money was kept separate in a trust. Senator Sean Bell on Friday said he did not know how Hanson funded the trip, before saying it was not with the campaign donations. “You’re asking me to speculate on something that I have no knowledge about,” Bell told News24 on Friday. “That money that we’ve raised, for instance, with the Fire the Liar campaign, I know for a fact that that is cordoned off where it can only be used to campaign against this terrible Albanese Labor government. All the money that was sent to that is being used on that issue,” he said.

“I can assure people, and Senator Hanson assures people, when we go overseas, we do so making sure people get bang for their buck. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson had earlier accused Hanson of betraying her supporters. “We have people who donate to her party from their limited savings, they’re struggling to get ahead, and now we find it’s going towards luxury hotel rooms in London, Dolce and Gabbana fashion shows,” Wilson told Nine’s Today. title: Bunnings has sucked me in … and taught me some lessons
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyConsumer spending Opinion Bunnings has sucked me in … and taught me some lessons Millie Muroi Economics Writer August 7, 2026 — 11:59am

August 7, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m a sucker for all things cute and fluffy – not adjectives you’d typically use when talking about a hardware store. It’s probably one of the reasons I rarely swing by Bunnings. Type “fluffy” into the search bar on Bunnings’ website, and you get washing liquid, dog beds and rugs. All very practical, but not very appealing for someone who finds enjoyment in impractical things. I’m hoping these bears will be an unconventional type of investment. One thing (arguably of many) that I never grew out of is my love of soft toys. I have far too many occupying far too much real estate on my bed for someone who has been an adult for nearly a decade. Now, they’ve been joined by Bunnings-branded … bears. Basically, Bunnings has cracked a code that has allowed it to expand into some new markets. Think: children, collectors … and at least one twenty-something woman who doesn’t especially need anything from Bunnings – least of all, another soft toy with diminishing marginal benefit.

Advertisement

“Blind boxes” – sealed packages containing random collectible items – have been around for a while, but in recent years, they’ve really taken off. Labubus, Sonny Angels and Smiskis are some of the most popular ones globally. Local stores such as Woolworths (with its Disney-themed “Ooshies”) have understood this lure of the unknown for a long time, taking advantage of the psychology driving our decision-making in their sales promotions. For a while, I thought I’d escaped the hold of blind boxes: none of them really appealed to me. While blind boxes aren’t technically counted as gambling because you don’t, strictly speaking, lose money (you always get something in return), the psychology works almost identically. And, arguably, despite ending up with 11 plush bears from Bunnings’ line-up – including some duplicates – I like to think I largely evaded their blind box “trap” and snagged a bargain. Either way, there are several economics lessons I took away from the experience. It all started with exposure. Unboxing videos have become increasingly popular on social media, with influencers opening products they’ve ordered or been sent, including the growing range of blind boxes.

Advertisement

The first few times I saw the Bunnings bears, I didn’t think much of them. Cute, but not necessary, I remember thinking. But there’s something called the “exposure effect”: a psychological tendency for people to develop a greater liking for things – whether it’s products or even people – the more they see them. It’s one of the reasons companies pay for advertising. They don’t just do it to make customers aware that their products exist, but also to develop brand recognition and familiarity which makes us more likely to reach for those items when shopping. Related Article Good Weekend ‘You can tell the fakes by the number of teeth’: My counterfeit Labubu conundrum It’s one of the ways that what we might think are rational decisions are not always as clear-cut as traditional economic models might assume. Often, our behaviours are influenced in ways that may not be rational or optimal for our wellbeing. That’s why there’s a relatively new branch of the discipline called “behavioural economics”: the study of how psychology, emotions and cognitive biases shape financial and economic decisions. The line-up of different Bunnings bears – each with a nearly one-in-four chance of being “pulled” from any given box – was cute, but it was the one marketed as the “secret bear” (with a one-in-16 chance of being found) that caught my eye.

Advertisement

The “sausage sizzle bear” is a teddy bear wrapped in a slice of (fake) bread to resemble the iconic Bunnings sausage sizzle snags. Clearly, not everyone would be swayed by this as much as I was. But it’s a good example of the effect of nostalgia: another thing that can increase our willingness to pay. Why? Because nostalgia is often linked to happy experiences and a sense of security. Pairing the cute teddy bear – which many of us already link to nostalgia – with an experience many of us are familiar with helps increase its appeal … at least for people like me. Related Article Retail The new status symbol for Gen Z is not what you’d expect Bunnings also created an artificial scarcity by making only a relatively small number of some of the bears. Generally, things that are finder to hard, or limited in quantity, are seen as more valuable. That’s why diamonds or vintage items, for example, tend to sell for eye-wateringly high prices. This scarcity is also the reason that the “sausage sizzle” bear has much higher asking prices from sellers on second-hand platforms such as Facebook Marketplace, Depop and eBay.

Advertisement

Seeing the bears pop up on these platforms, I decided that rather than going to Bunnings and buying potentially dozens of blind boxes (retailing for $12.50 each) to find the one I wanted, I was probably better off buying one someone had already found – even if it meant paying significantly more. I settled for a sausage sizzle bear off Facebook Marketplace which was selling for $50: probably a better-value option than testing my luck with blind boxes and ending up spending lots of money with double-ups of bears I didn’t have a huge desire for, I thought. Of course, the appeal of blind boxes is largely the element of surprise: not knowing what you might get. While blind boxes aren’t technically counted as gambling because you don’t, strictly speaking, lose money (you always get something in return), the psychology works almost identically. Humans tend to enjoy a bit of uncertainty because it can boost excitement and trigger a bigger dopamine rush. Plenty of people have probably gone to Bunnings to buy these blind boxes for that very experience. From Bunnings’ perspective, they bring a lot of value. Not only does it probably make a tidy profit from them (the bears would cost much less than $12.50 to manufacture), but they also bring foot traffic to its stores from people who might be tempted to pick up a few other things while they’re there.

Advertisement

Collectible items can also drive consumption in other ways. When I first bought the sausage sizzle bear, I thought that would be the end. It was all I wanted. But the thing about collectibles is that they exploit psychological triggers such as completion bias: the tendency for people to feel compelled to complete something once they’ve started it. Loading When I found someone selling the full set of Bunnings bears for $60 on Facebook Marketplace, I jumped at the opportunity. Partly, it was driven by the idea that maybe, just maybe, it could be an investment. Most full sets I had seen in the secondhand market were fetching at least $100, and surely when the next instalment of bears is released, there will be people willing to pay a higher price for a complete set, I remember thinking. But there’s also something called the endowment effect: a tendency to overvalue (and justify) items once we own them. While I’m yet to see many people selling a full set of the bears for less than $100, it’s also very possible they will be worthless in a year or two.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Pay What Macca’s reveals about our living standards – and how to get a free lunch Millie Muroi Economics Writer Nonetheless, I also ended up buying a bear from the first collection of Bunnings bears (released last year), which then led to me buying another four for $30 from a woman on Depop. Part of me thought it could add to my “investment”, but there was also a part of me itching to complete the two sets. Awareness of these cognitive and behavioural biases can help us be a bit more rational in our spending, and bring us closer to the neat models of traditional economics, which are built on the assumption we always make optimal decisions. While there are a handful of the ultra-rare “hoodie” bears from the first Bunnings collection (which would complete my two sets) on online secondhand marketplaces, most of them seem to have an asking price of at least $150 as a standalone item. That’s probably not an optimal use of money for anyone, let alone someone with a mortgage. And even for an irrational consumer like me, I’ve decided that’s a bit steep … or is it? title: ‘Snatched’ in Turkey: How a gory social media trend is fuelling a surge in cosmetic tourism
text:
While Australians increasingly film their post-op journeys for millions of views, doctors are scrambling to build a national database to measure the strain botched overseas surgeries are placing on our healthcare system.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Joanne McGinnis always hated the excess skin on her neck. At the hairdresser, she felt self-conscious when the salon cape was fastened snugly, gathering the loose skin underneath her chin. “I hated looking in the mirror,” she said. “My biggest insecurity was my neck.” Joanne McGinniss paid $18,000 for extensive cosmetic surgery in Turkey. She is far from alone. In February this year, for her 45th birthday, McGinniss boarded a plane to Turkey. The purpose of the trip? “Getting snatched,” she said. She is far from alone. In the past 18 months, Australian plastic surgeons have observed a striking uptick in people travelling to Turkey for cheap, fast-tracked cosmetic procedures, including facelifts and hair transplants.

Advertisement

The surge in cosmetic tourism has spurred a troubling wave of post-surgical complications and an online trend where patients document their recovery process on Instagram and TikTok. Related Article Cosmetic Cowboys Crackdown on deceptive social media posts by cosmetic doctors In the “recovery diary” videos, patients who have travelled to the cosmetic surgery hotspot of Istanbul document their swollen, bruised, bloodied, bandaged faces, gruesome complications and emotional ups and downs in daily instalments. McGinniss said she shared her story online to provide insights on her recovery and tips on how to find a credible and safe surgeon. She said she is not paid for her content, framing it as a free public service to support anyone considering or recovering from cosmetic surgery. Her inbox is flooded with messages. “I can’t keep up, it’s like a second job,” she said.

Advertisement

The Adelaide woman went from 600 followers to more than 18,500 almost overnight. Some of her videos now have more than three million views. “The first few weeks were really quite difficult,” she said of her recovery. “I was like ‘holy shit! What have I done?’ Because you just don’t look like you and then every time you’re looking in the mirror, you’re questioning yourself.” Joanne McGinniss in the days after her extensive cosmetic surgery. But Australian doctors say they are increasingly having to pick up the pieces when these overseas surgeries go wrong. Australian Society for Plastic Surgeons president Dr Brigid Corrigan said in severe cases, doctors have treated permanently damaged nerves, dead skin, bleeding, wound infections, abnormal scarring and asymmetry that required revision surgery. “We are really seeing the full spectrum of complications,” Corrigan said. Concerned by this trend, the peak body has started to compile data on botched procedures and complications in a national database, which is also tracking hospital admissions.

Advertisement

They warn patients are being lured by cosmetic surgery packages that include five-star hotels and VIP airport transfers that allow them to squeeze in as many surgeries as possible within a short timeframe. Related Article Ageing A facelift under 40: Is it worth it? McGinniss estimates she saved about $80,000 getting her surgery abroad, spending more than a year carefully researching surgeons in Turkey before finally booking one in. While McGinniss said many people supported the online documentation of her recovery, she was trolled by a small group of followers, who told her she looked older post-facelift and needed a “hair transplant”. Then came the death threats. “I got a message that was... saying like, ‘die you f---ing slut’. Just terrible stuff,” she said. “You just think, ‘wow,’ but it says more about those people than it does about anyone else.”

Advertisement

McGinniss is happy with the result of her surgery and said she’d had minimal complications. Joanne McGinniss is happy with the results of her surgery and says she had minimal complications. But not all are so lucky. One Australian woman recently documented her physically gruelling recovery from a hotel room in Turkey after having a facelift, which left her skin puckered and her eyes cat-like, grotesque and asymmetrical. “You just have to trust the process,” she told her tens of thousands of followers. “Trust the process” is a common phrase used by those documenting their stories online, and positing videos of themselves at airports and waking up in hospital beds hooked up to plastic tubes. Sometimes, they film content with their beaming surgeons beside them; a way to promote the cosmetic clinics and receive discounted procedures.

title: New plan to help 300 people a night as more Aussies forced into tents: 'It's about dignity'
text:
A Queensland charity supporting people experiencing homelessness is expanding its frontline response, with a donated ambulance set to become a mobile healthcare clinic for hundreds of Australians sleeping rough.

Nourish Street founder and president Beau Haywood told Yahoo News that demand for the charity's outreach services has surged in recent months, with its Brisbane city runs now supporting between 260 and 300 people each outreach.

The organisation's Moreton Bay service has also grown to around 170 people, up from about 70 around 18 months ago.

Advertisement Advertisement

The donated ambulance, which Beau estimates would have cost about $70,000, will allow Nourish Street to provide medical support in a more private and dignified setting.

"It's about dignity," Beau said.

"By having a mobile healthcare clinic, we can actually dress these things in a more hygienic situation, as well as a more dignified way."

Beau said healthcare has become an increasingly important part of the charity's work as more people arrive at outreach events with chronic illnesses, infections and other medical issues. Source: Supplied

From roadside treatment to a mobile clinic

The ambulance will initially focus on the charity's Redcliffe outreach before expanding into Brisbane city once a week.

The service will provide wound care, health assessments, referrals and medical advice, with plans to eventually offer additional services including immunisations and hepatitis checks.

Beau said healthcare has become an increasingly important part of the charity's work as more people arrive at outreach events with chronic illnesses, infections and other medical issues.

Beau recently acquired 98 tents worth about $6,000 for people sleeping rough. Source: Supplied

"A lot of these people won't go and get that help until it becomes almost life-threatening," he said.

He said some people experiencing homelessness avoid hospitals or doctors due to previous experiences or concerns about how they will be treated.

"At the moment, we do it on the side of our vehicle," he said.

"People will be able to have these discussions in private rather than in public around the side of the vehicle."

The growing demand has also put pressure on the charity's ability to provide basic essentials, with Beau recently collecting 98 tents worth about $6,000 for people sleeping rough.

He said the supply would likely last less than a month, with tents only providing a temporary solution for people without shelter.

"A tent's not made for permanent living," Beau added.

"They leak, they rip, they tear. But even if someone got two weeks out of a $70 tent, it's $5 a night for accommodation, and you can't really get cheaper than that."

More Aussies pushed onto the streets

The charity's increased workload comes as Beau says the profile of people seeking support has changed significantly.

He said that while addiction was once a major factor among many people accessing the service, rising living costs and a lack of affordable rentals have pushed more Australians into homelessness.

"We're seeing a lot more families, a lot more elderly people and a lot more working people that are still trying to hold down a job while now living rough," he said.

"People can actually afford to rent, they just can't find one."
